speechtext: Hon. FRANK COCHRANE (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 237, respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, and the Toronto Harbour Commissioners.
Explain.

The first order of the Railway Commission was for a four-track viaduct, but it was considered that this would not be sufficient to carry the traffic in Toronto. They reconsidered their order, and are to make an order for six tracks, but moving out to the water's edge. This Bill is authority to the different parties who are interested, including the city of Toronto, to expropriate between the track and the water. The* Harbour Commissioners in Toronto are in favour of this, in order to facilitate the development of the harbour.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (acting Minister of the Interior):
speechtext:
Yesterday my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) asked a question concerning some complaints made respecting the treatment received by certain Russians passing through Moosejaw and other points on the Canadian Pacific railway. The Prime Minister partially answered the question yesterday, and promised that I would refer to it to-day. Early in April, we received direct from Moosejaw a complaint touching this matter. Later we received a complaint from the Russian Consul General at Montreal. We also received a complaint from the Trades and Labour Council of Moosejaw. We then had the matter investigated by the Commissioner of Immigration at Winnipeg, who reports on April 12, as follows:
Press reports regarding Russian labourers' incident at Boharom, Sask., entirely inaccurate and grossly misleading. For information of Russian Consul General at (Montreal beg to say that on April 2, special train containing four hundred Russian labourers left Moosejaw for western points on Canadian Pacific railway destined railroad construction. Fellow countrymen at Moosejaw had incited Russian labourers to break contract, desert employment and find work independently. In order to prevent this desertion, cars locked at Moosejaw, train passing Boharm at speed of twenty miles an hour when seventeen labourers succeeded opening doors, jumped from fast moving train and endeavoured to escape. Guard stopped train; ordered Russians to return; fired revolver into air to intimidate them. No person struck by bullets; three persons slightly injured by leaping from moving train. Statement regarding food and other improper action against Russians entirely unfounded. The men were not locked in cars except when passing through terminals and divisional points, and no attempt' was made to attack them and no injury sustained except already above indicated.
We communicated the contents of that report to the Imperial Russian Consul General at Montreal, and received the following letter from him:
I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your communication of the 16th of this month, in answer to my telegram of the 9th, addressed to the Honourable the Minister of the Interior, in connection with the shooting that occurred under peculiar circumstances, when a party of Russian subjects left Moosejaw for Boharm, Sask., on the 2nd of April of this year, by special train.
Please accept my sincere thanks for your kind reply, the details of which have been duly appreciated by me.
There being no doubt, however, that the shooting took place, I beg leave to ask whether such a course is allowed under the given circumstances and is authorized by law, as a coercive measure.
The matter of the conduct of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in connection with this incident is receiving further consideration. That is all I desire to say at present concerning the matter.

While the statement of the minister that the action of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is receiving further consideration at the hands of the department may be satisfactory, I would like it to be considered that that assertion on the part of the minister does not close the matter. It is desirable that at a later date the minister shall make a further statement as to the result of his dealings with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in regard to this matter. The Russian consul has made a suggestion, which, I think, should appeal to the mind of everybody, that the action cannot be condoned.

I see that the deputy
minister's salary is ptit down here at $5,000. I have noticed in the estimates that the salaries of some of the deputy ministers have been considerably increased, some of them exceeding the amount provided for those officers in the Civil Service Act. I do not object to the payment of proper salaries to deputy ministers; but, when the salary of the deputy of one department is increased, it may be difficult to convince the deputy ministers of other departments that they are -not equally entitled to larger salaries. The deputy ministers of Railways and of Public Works have to perform very heavy tasks and assume great responsibilities. The Deputy Minister of Railways has for years been chairman of the Government Railways Managing Board, and has assumed many other worries and cares in connection with the Intercolonial railway, but his salary remains at $5,000. I thought it well to call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that he will get into trouble unless he divides the officials of the department into classes, assigning a specific salary to each class, and, perhaps, giving a greater salary to those officials whose duties are the most onerous. I think that is done by the British Government, and as long as the deputy ministers of the departments are on a common level so far as salaries are concerned, I think my hen. friend will experience some difficulty. I think the deputy ministers, particularly in the very busy departments, are not paid sufficient salaries, and I would prefer that my remarks should he accepted as having been made from that standpoint than from

the standpoint of criticism of any increases.
What about the members?

I appreciate very much what the hon. member has said in respect to the salaries of deputies; but, as my hon. friend well knows, it is a very difficult matter to deal with. I quite agree that there are certain deputy ministers to-day whose salaries are not nearly sufficient for the amount of work they have to do. There were special circumstances in the case of the Deputy Minister of Justice, whose services, owing to his long and high standing in the legal profession, it was impossible for us to retain unless his salary was increased, and the position would have been very difficult to fill. At the same time, the question of the salaries of certain other deputies has had consideration in the way of suggested increases; but, in view of the complicated nature of the Civil Service Act, if I may say so, it was difficult, during a busy session, to arrive at any conclusion. This is a matter that will be further considered; in fact, I think before long it will be necessary to reconsider the whole Civil Service Act. I am sorry that my hon. friend did not go a little further when he had in his mind, I know, to suggest that the salaries of other people in this House should be increased as well as the salaries of deputy ministers. However, I think that is a matter that will toe considered later on.

So far as the deputy Minister of Justice is concerned, I am rather inclined to think that, from the standpoint of his ability and the work that he is doing in the department and for the country generally, his salary has not been sufficiently increased. His position does not at all resemble that of other deputy ministers. The deputy Minister of Justice acts as counsel for the Crown in, I think, all cases going before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. He is capable of filling that position, as capable perhaps as any man you could get at the English Bar. He has relieved this country from the payment of enormous counsel fees to eminent counsel in England by reason of his capability to take the cases before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London. I submit that the position of Deputy Minister of Justice is not at all similar to that of other deputy ministers, and that he should be in a class apart. If we are to have as Deputy Minister of Justice a man who is capable of filling the position and taking the briefs for the Government, as the present deputy does, then he should be paid absolutely in a class apart from the deputy ministers of other departments. I have nothing to say in regard to what a deputy minister Mr. GRAHAM.
should receive. I do not think that they should all be paid similar salaries, because the official duties of some are far more responsible than those of others. I think there should toe a vast distinction. However, I wish to record my suggestion that the Deputy Minister of Justice is getting not more than he should receive, tout less.

The only objection I
have to the inequality of salary of the deputy ministers is that the deputy Minister of the Naval Service is being paid $6,000 while the Deputy Minister of Public Works receives only $5,000. The Deputy Minister of Public Works has certainly more important duties than the deputy Minister of the Naval Service. What existed of the Naval Service before this date is rapidly sinking into oblivion, and if it keeps on, very soon the Deputy Minister of the-Naval Service will have nothing to do, whilst the Deputy Minister of Public Works is filling a very important position, perhaps the most important of all the positions as executive heads of departments. The minister will realize himself that his department is a most important one.
Of course.

The minister has soared up from the Department of the Interior to the Department of Public WoTks, and if it were not more important he would have remained in his old place. I cannot see why his deputy should be paid only $5,000 when the Deputy Minister of the Naval Service is paid $6,000 for doing practically nothing.

That is only another instance of the many inequalities and anomalies in the Civil Service Act which we found when we took it over, and which I think we must find some way of remedying in the near future.

There is another inequality shown in the supplementary estimates. It is proposed to raise the salary of the assistant deputy minister of another department to the same figure as the Deputy Minister of Public Works. In the supplemen-taries there is an item to increase the salary of the assistant deputy minister and secretary of the Department of Justice to $5,000. That, I suppose, will be explained by the Minister of Justice when we come to it, tout I draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to this item. He has told the committee that there are inequalities which need to be adjusted, and that item is one of the most glaring of these inequalities. In connection with the remark that it would be difficult to retain the services of the Deputy Minister of Justice unless his salary were increased, as to which I express no opinion at the moment, I would point out that a few years ago,

when a similar state of things occurred with reference to the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, the 'Government allowed the gentleman then occupying that position to resign from the seervice rather than grant him an increase in salary.

I think that is not a
good argument to make, that the deputy minister will not stay in office unless his salary is increased; I think it is a kind of hold-up of the minister. If the present deputy minister does not want to stay in office I think the minister will he able to find many other men who could occupy the position. By increasing the salary of the Deputy Minister of Justice by $3,000 we are going to create discontent among the other deputy ministers. They will feel that they are underpaid, and there will be disorganization of the whole service. My hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) says that the deputy minister takes briefs before the Privy Council. I know he has done so in the past, but I understand that in the most important cases the department has engaged the services of eminent counsel. The reference to the Supreme Court in the marriage case was in the hands of eminent counsel from Toronto and Montreal, and when the case was argued before the Privy Council those counsel went there. The case was not in the hands of the Deputy Minister of Justice. The department pays every year large sums of money in legal fees for the employment of counsel to plead either in the Supreme Court or before the Privy Council, and I think there is no necessity of increasing the salary of the deputy minister by $3,000.

I may be allowed to say a word in this respect. I know that we cannot discuss the question of salaries generally at the present moment; but, starting from the head of this House-I occupied that honourable position for a short time- I want to point out the anomaly that the Speaker is paid $4,000 and is supposed to entertain people from the whole Dominion. The Clerk of the House is paid $5,000. The Clerk is not sufficiently paid; so far as the Speaker is concerned, I leave the House to judge. We have in the Minister of Justice one of the most gifted men in his profession, but he will receive $3,000 less than his deputy. What impression will this create in the public mind? What about the members of Parliament who spend five, six or seven months of the year in Ottawa attending to public business? I Came the other day from western Canada in company with one of the highest officials in the service of the Dominion, who had been attending to public business in Washington. He expressed the opinion that a member of the House of Commons of Canada, if he was fit for the position, was the equal of
a member of Congress in the United States. The members of the Administration know that members of Congress in the United States are paid much more than members of the House of Commons in Canada. He expressed the opinion that $5,000 would not be too much to pay a competent member of the House of Commons to remain here for six or seven months of the year and work for his constituency and for the country. I am speaking Tather freely, because I have been here for fourteen years, and I have seen the House change complexion two or three times. It has come to this, that only the rich man or the very poor man can afford to come here. It is impossible for the active business man, or the active professional man to come here and spend six or seven months of the year. The rich man can afford to come as a luxury, or as an honour; but the poor man, if he retains the confidence of the electors, is in fifteen or twenty years practically out on the street. There have been men occupying seats in the House of Commons, who to-day would be in the poor house but for the fact that they are paid, in one way or another, from the public treasury, i think the Administration should look seriously into this question and begin at the top. If a member of the Cabinet, with the responsibilities that rest upon him, is worth anything to the people he should receive a larger salary than that which is paid to him at the present time. The present salary is ridiculous. There is any number of third-class officials in some of the large firms in Montreal who receive a larger salary than that paid to ministers of the Crown in Canada. I should be glad to see the Minister of Public Works and his colleagues take up this question, face it, and solve it satisfactorily, beginning with the members of the Cabinet, senators, members of the House of Commons, going down through the Civil Service, and giving proper payment to those who give proper service.

I want to say a word on this question as to the increase of salary. The Minister of Public Works has said that it would not be possible to increase the salary of the Deputy Minister of Public. Works on account of the Civil Service Act. It seems to me that that should have (been looked into before, because I claim that the Public Works Department is the most important department of the Government, and if anyone should get an increase of salary it is the Deputy Minister of Public Works. I was never against an increase of salary. It has been my ambition, sffice I was able to work, to increase my salary. Of course there will be some members who believe they are not earning more than they are getting, in the way of an indemnity, at the present time. I claim I am earning more,



and it seems to me that the Government should take into consideration the question of increasing the indemnity to some extent, so as to make it reasonable, and so that our position would be looked upon as a reasonable one. There are many men who can well afford to come here, men with large businesses of their own, or men who are favoured with fortune but I am not in that position at all. Probably I am in a better position to discuss this question than some members, for this reason: the year before I came here the indemnity was increased from $1,500 to $2,500, and during the first session I was in the House a Bill was introduced for the repeal of that increase. I did not vote in favour of the increase at that time, not being in the House, but I spoke against the Bill. for the reduction. I stated then, as I state now, that I do not know of any man with common sense who would be against an increase of the indemnity, or salary. I call it a salary, because it is _ a salary, however small it may be. Having heard rumours around the corridors, I was expecting that an increase would be agreed upon this session. It might be said that an increase would not be popular throughout the country. I for one am willing to defend it in any part of the country where I have a chance to do so. We are worth more money than we are getting to-day, or we are worth nothing at all. We spend six or seven months of the year legislating in the interests of the people, and safeguarding the interests of the country, and I believe that the sessions cannot be any shorter than six months in the future. The country is growing all the time, and the development of the country forces on legislation from year to year in increasing volume. With the very best will on the part of the members to expedite business, I do not see how it is possible in the future, having regard to the growth of the country, to have shorter sessions than the one we have had this year. In these circumstances, I do not see how any members on either side of the House can say they are willing to come here, and spend six or seven months for the salary they are receiving to-day. It seems to me that the Minister of Public Works should do something this session, and I hope the rumours I have heard around the corridors will materialize before the session is finished.

I regret to say that the tendency is to Increase the salaries of the better fiaid officials, of the higher officials, while the Government will employ a messenger in a department at $500 a year. How can you expect a man to support a family on a salary of $500 a year ? The officer who gets $5,000 a year is eon-Mr. VF.RVILLE.
sidered worthy of an increase of salary, and one who" gets $7,000 a year wants it increased to $10,000 a year.
A man should not have any family if he has only $500 a year. .
I do noc agree with the hon. member for Frontenao. Every man should have the privilege of getting married. Why should you penalize a man because he has not the education to occupy a higher position ?
Do you mean to say that if a man is not married he is penalized ?

I think the tendency is to increase the higher salaries and not to consider the officials who are not well paid. They may not be underpaid for the work they do, but still they have to live, and they have to support a family, and they should be paid enough to enable them to do so. There should be greater equalization in the salaries of the service. So far as the members' sessional indemnity is concerned, it has always been considered an indemnity, and not a salary. If it were a salary I would be of opinion that- it should be increased, but as it is an indemnity, so far as I am concerned I shall be against any increase.

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to take part in this debate concerning the increase of salaries; but as some hon. members to the left have taken this, opportunity to ask for an increase of parliamentary indemnity, I must say, first, that as far as I am concerned I who, at the last election,, preached for economy and for a plebiscite on any new expenditure, I would like the members from the province of Quebec, especially, to say if they are in favour of an indemnity of $4,000 to $5,000 per session. Should such an increase be granted, it would mean an additional expenditure of $817,500 to pay the members of the Lower and of the Upper House, which sum represents a capital of $20,000,000 at 4 per cent interest.
I think that, with this sum of 20 millions, splendid results could be achieved for the welfare of the country, which would be much more expedient than to increase the salaries without consulting the people. 1 may say that, for my part, I shall be against those increases of salaries as long as the people have not been consulted.
Would the minister explain the increase in the number of employees in his department from 311 last year to 336 this year?

The principal increase is in the architect's department. Heretofore it has been the practice of the Public Works Department to let out the planning of public buildings in different parts of Canada. We are now endeavouring to have a sufficient number of architects and draughtsmen to carry on the work here. The architects have studied out the plans upon which public buildings best meet the public service, and we can draw the plans better, cheaper and more efficiently in the department than we can have them prepared by letting them out.

Mr. Chairman, I have heard the remarks which the 350i
hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Lanctot) has just made. I must tell him that, for my part, I have already stated what I think about this, subject of parliamentary indemnity.
When we were discussing the question of granting an increase of salary to the Chairman of the Railway Commission a week or two ago, I declared that those salaries were not in proportion with those paid to the members of this House; that it was ridiculous to pay us $2,500 a year when we have to remain at Ottawa six or seven months in the year, looking after the business of the country, and then taking the balance of the year to attend to public business in our respective counties. Moreover, I spoke to several members from the province of Quebec about this, and I must say that those Whom I have spoken to are all in favour of increasing the indemnity.
I have heard the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), and I must say that they bear the stamp of common sense.
Really, this increase of salaries in behalf of the deputy ministers cannot be justified. The intention is to give them a higher salary than the ministers themselves are getting; this seems to me extraordinary. After all, it is the ministers who are responsible for the administration of the country's.business, they are called upon to meet the requirements of the position, and I say that the salary of a minister, at $7,000 a year, is not proportionate at all, if a deputy minister's own salary is raised to $10^000. It is proposed to raise the salary of the Deputy Minister of Justice to $10,000 a year because of his legal experience and of his being obliged to go to England and plead the Government's cases.
Those expenses are paid outside of his salary.
I would admit that increase if he paid, his travelling expenses and if he got no salary here while he was absent; but I think his salary runs just the same.
His travelling expenses are paid outside of his halary.

If those travelling expenses are paid outside of his salary, I think that is a little too much; we should be more cautious.
I knpw an employee who works here for the country at the rate of $3 a day and who does the work of a man whose salary is $2,000 a year. That employee does the work just as well as the other and never theless he only get $3 a day.
I wonder if the increase of salaries can warrant a better service. It is always easier

to reduce the salary of a man than to raise *it. It seems to me, therefore, that we should stop and think before increasing the srI^tIbs
As I have said a couple of weeks ago, when the question of increasing the salary of the Chairman of the Railway Commission was under consideration, we, members of *this House, do not get more than $2,500, and we are here for six or seven months in the year, as the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Verville) has remarked. Moreover, when we are 'back at home we keep busy for the rest of the year, working in the interest of our counties as much as we do here during the session. Therefore, it is for all the year that this indemnity is given.
As to the public servants in general,
,-our every day's experience is there to back my statement-we seldom find them at their office more than four hours a day. Besides that, they get one month or two months' vacation every year, and their salaries run just the same. As for the members of this House, they get no holidays.
I am against this idea of increasing the salaries, especially those of high-graded employees. As for the employees of an inferior rank, many of them are not sufficiently paid as compared with the others, and, moreover, they are the ones who do the hardest work. Therefore I believe that we should not vote that increase of salary which it is the intention to grant to certain public employees.

I am not speaking for the society, but as a citizen, and I would ask the minister to consider in the plans for the new building the providing of accommodation for the meetings of the Royal Society, and a suitable place where they could have their library and keep their archives.

Mr. Chairman, I approve of the words which have just fallen from the lips of my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux).
We receive, at the present time, the most distinguished men of science and of letters in Canada. These men are making sacrifices for the honour of Canada. I would feel most happy if the desire expressed by my friend from Rouville could be yielded to.

At present we are
cramped for space, so that it is impossible for us to be very generous to a request made by the Royal Society or any other body. I understand the Royal Society have not asked for any space of this kind. They did ask and were granted space for their library in the Museum building, and of course when requests of that kind are made we shall always be glad, even in our cramped condition, or when the new public buildings are completed, to facilitate as far as we can the meetings of the Royal Society in Ottawa.

Is there provision for
modern ventilation in the new buildings which will be erected? In any of the Government buildings that I have been in, in Ottawa-I have not been in many-there is no system of ventilation except opening the windows. If these new buildings are properly ventilated we might go over and sit in them occasionally, so as to regain our lost health.

We are endeavouring to
provide in the new buildings the very best possible system of ventilation. We are taking care that the plans shall be the best that it is possible for us to obtain. We have asked the Canadian Society of Architects to name one of their number, and they have already suggested their president, Mr. Russell. We have asked the English Institute of Architects to be good enough to name for us a representative, and they have already done so. The Government will select a third, and these three gentlemen will have full charge of the plans, which are open to competition of architects in all parts of the British Empire.
Will these three gentlemen select the plans?

When we get the plans
from the competitors, these three gentlefor

.nen will select the best ones.
What is the estimated cost of that building?
There are several buildings.
You are speaking now of the new buildings, not of this building here?
Yes. We cannot give an estimate until the plans are selected. The cost will be five or six million dollars, perhaps more.
Is any provision made for enlarging the library?

No, there is nothing in
the estimates for that this year.

The librarians have been asking for more room for the last ten or fifteen years. Every year the Library Committee makes the report that books have to be stored in the cellar, and that those which cannot be stored have to be destroyed. They are cramped in every way, and some provision will have to be made very soon, either by the construction of a new library or an enlargement of the present one. I understand the objection to that is that the ground is rather small.
I find we have an item in the estimates for an enlargement or what we call a wing to the Senate, and it will provide accommodation for a good part of the library.
In regard to these new buildings, I would like to ask under what conditions the labourers will have to work. Will the contract be let on an eight-hour day system?
We have not got to the point of considering that question yet-this is the first I have heard of it. It will be fully considered when we come to let the contract.	.

My hon. friend did not
say anything about the ventilation of the eastern departmental block.

I thought my hon. friend was referring to the proposed new buildings. In regard to the building which has just been erected, we have made a special effort to obtain good ventilation, and we believe the system is working fairly well.
If it is satisfactory, I assume the hon. Minister of Public Works will apply it to this House.
Yes. We have made an effort this session to get good ventilation in this Chamber, and I would like to know from hon. members whether or not there has been any improvement.
Yes.

The system was not very expensive, but we thought we would try it and see if it would be of some assistance.
I would like to know, because we had this change made on condition that if it was not satisfactory we would not have to pay for it. We are now at the point whether it is worth settling for or not.

I have no objection to
offer. The smell of the ozone was rather strong at first.
That was the first day or two, before the machine was put into proper working order. I think it has been found fairly satisfactory to hon. members.
My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works does not often deserve congratulation, but I think he deserves some congratulation for this improvement in the ventilation of this chamber.

I see that the hon. minister proposes to get architects and others conversant with the subject of ventilation to establish the best system of ventilation possible. I have met some of the very best architects who thought that they had discovered the very best system, but the practical man, who has done the work himself, sometimes can give very valuable information. I would suggest to the Minister of Public Works that he should consult some sound, practical men on this subject.

As far as this Chamber is concerned, if any hon. member can suggest any means by which we can improve the ventilation, I feel it would be our duty to carry out his suggestions. As Minister of Public Works, I am prepared to try almost anything by which we can improve the condition of the air in this Chamber. If my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) will suggest a practical man who will supply the remedy, that apparently the architects and those conversant with matters of ventilation have been unable to supply so far, we shall be glad to avail ourselves of his services.

I would like to suggest that this carpet, while it is a pretty one, should be removed and be replaced by linoleum. I do not think it is sanitary or healthy in a Chamber where there is so much speaking going on and members are moving around constantly. Dust is rising all the time, and it is impossible to have a sanitary condition of affairs so long as we have a carpet on the floor. I would suggest to ,the hon. minister that he take the necessary steps during the summer to have this condition remedied.
What about the noise?

I made a suggestion some years ago, which has never been accepted either by the late Minister of Public Works or by the present one, that is, that the windows be opened. I would like to make the suggestion now in this form, that the windows be opened whenever the House rises at night and remain open until the House sits again.

The windows are opened at night now. When I first had them opened a little earlier in the session, as they are on that side of the House, I was accused by certain lion, gentlemen of trying to injure their health, and I promptly had them closed.

Can my hon. friend
give us any information as to where the new departmental buildings proposed to be built in Ottawa are to be located?
The plans have been on exhibition in the Railway Committee room for some weeks.
Have these plans been accepted?
Yes, and they have been published in the papers as well.
I think the location is a good one, and, as far as I can see, the plans are quite satisfactory. What is the size of the building now being put up between Mackenzie avenue and Sussex street?
80 feet wide and 320 feet long. It occupies the full width of the block.
Is the space which is left vacant to be added-to Major's Hill park?

That is the idea. There was at first some objection to our building in that locality at all, but, after giving the matter careful consideration, we thought that the erection of such a nice building as we propose to build there, and the sodding and earing for the ground not occupied would tend to beautify the place.

Are the Supreme and
Exchequer Courts to be located in the new building on Mackenzie avenue?
No, they will be in the new departmental buildings on Wellington street.

May I make a suggestion to my hon. friend? These grounds on Sussex street were at first taken by the late government with the intention of putting up certain buildings, and it was then suggested to us that, instead of being put there they should be built upon the site selected by my hon. friend, and Mr. WILSON (Laval).	-
that we should add the grounds on Sussex street to Major's Hill park. I would not have been sorry if this plan had been carried out; but perhaps the erection of such a building as is contemplated may do very well on such a street. I would suggest that it would be well for my hon. friend at the earliest moment to remove the Printing Bureau from where it is now and add the ground thus left vacant to Major's Hill park, or to Nepean Point park. The Printing Bureau was built as a temporary structure; it is not at all beautiful, and I think it would be better located elsewhere. Some time ago I asked my hon. friend whether it was intended that Major's Hill park should be used only by pedestrians or whether vehicles would be allowed upon it. The hon. gentleman told me that he would look into the matter. I do not know whether or not he has had time to do so, but I see some objection to having this park open to vehicular traffic. I think Mackenzie avenue might be improved by joining it to the roadway running from Nepean Point towards Rideau Hall. At the present time the avenue is blocked up with materials being used by the contractors at work on the Sussex street buildings, and I think that these materials should be removed, and Mackenzie avenue made such as it should be.

In view of the fact that the construction of this new building is going on, it may be difficult during the present summer to put Mackenzie avenue in proper shape. It is, however, our intention to put Mackenzie avenue in good condition and make it, instead of Sussex street, the regular driveway to Rideau Hall. Had it not been for the necessity of providing an entrance for teams with heavy wagon loads of goods we would have erected the customs warehouse on the new ground that we have just purchased; but it has not been considered advisable to have such a building on this new land. I will take a note' of what my hon. friend has said with regard to the Printing Bureau. It is certainly an eyesore; but while we are busy at something else we cannot attend to that. I agree with my hon. friend, however, in his suggestion that it should be removed. In respect to the park, we do not propose to allow vehicles to enter the park at all.

When the buildings
along Wellington street are completed, is it the intention of the Government to withdraw from the offices which are rented in various parts of the city?

That is the purpose for
which the buildings are to be Constructed.

In connection with the
suggestion which my hon. friend has just approved, namely, the removal of the Printing Bureau to a more desirable site,

might I remind my hon. friend that in the last estimates submitted to Parliament by the late government there was an item of $100,000 for the initial expenses in connection with the purchase of a new site. The site the then Government had in view was one I mentioned to my hon. friend the present Minister of the Interior, last session. It consists of two blocks bounded by Sussex and Dalhousie streets on the north and south, Botelier street on the east and Bingham Square on the west. It is known as the old St. Lawrence and Ottawa railway yard, and I do not think a more desirable site for the Printing Bureau could be obtained in or about Ottawa. 1 would suggest further that if the land purchased for the new buildings to be erected to the west of the present Parliament grounds terminates at its westerly boundary at what is known as the Perley property, my hon. friend should take into consideration the advisability of purchasing the narrow strip of land on the north side of Wellington street extending from .the boundary of the Perley property to what is known as Pooley's bridge. There are only a few houses on that strip of land; they are old and in a dilapidated condition, and the property will never be valuable for anything execpt as an addition to the land already purchased by the Government. If this land is not purchased, the present buildings or others of a temporary character that may be put there will be an eyesore and will detract very much from the appearance of the grounds and buildings when these are completed.

If the hon. gentleman
will notice the ground plans as they are in the Railway Department, he will see that there is a piece of ground at the corner known as the Perley home which does not appear to be in use so far as the present programme as laid out is concerned. Would not that, in addition to the strip mentioned by my hon. friend, be a good site for the Printing Bureau?

As a manufacturing
establishment the Printing Bureau would in many ways be objectionable if erected close to the new office buildings.

Has the minister a
plan which will show the proposed addition? We were fortunate enough, when adding the wing at the west of this building, not to impair the whole structure. The hon. member for

In round figures, about $229,000.
When the new buildings as proposed are completed, will the Government be able to house all their different departments, so as to pay no further rentals?

Yes, the space will be
sufficient to take care of all the departments that are now in rented offices.

Sometimes, when buildings are being erected for the Government, it is found that after the plan has been followed and the building completed, the departments which are to occupy the building desire to have changes made in it, and changes are made here and there, with the result that new work is torn down and no little expense incurred. That is not a reproach to the minister or to his department but it is a criticism of the method pursued. Certain architects make a specialty of interior designing in connection with large commercial buildings, that is, laying out the floor space so as to give the very greatest amount of accommodation. I would suggest that the services of such architects be invoked.
That matter was considered, and it is now in the hands of officers of the department with a view to working it out in such form as will be suitable to the different departments.
Is the customs building the only one that will occupy the new site on Sussex street?
We may be able to place one other department there.

Some years ago, when it was decided to erect new public buildings, I suggested to the then Minister of Public Works and to the chief architect the name of a young Canadian who has studied in Paris, and achieved success there. I refer to Mr. Marchand, who is the leading architect in the city of Montreal, I dare say in Canada. He has been selected by one or two American universities to rive courses of lectures, and in Montreal he has left his signature on at least two monumental buildings in which my hon. friend the minister when he visits Montreal might find inspiration. The late Minister of Public Works and the architect of the department agreed to give Mr. Marchand the architectural supervision of these new buildings, and, in view of that, he abstained from taking part in the competition. I have no brief for Mr. Marchand. I do not know what happened to the arrangement which was then entered into by '.he department and the chief architect. I simply say that Mr. Marchand is a credit to our country. He has testimonials from the highest authorities in Europe, and he might well be in a position to give his views to the department in the matter which now occupies the attention of the committee. I am sure that everybody who is familiar with his work will admit that Mr. Marchand is certainly the leading authority on architecture in this country, and the fact that he has been selected by American universities to give lectures, once cr twice a year.
Mr. ROGERS.
is the best evidence that his services are worthy of the attention of the minister.

We all appreciate the
ability of.Mr. Marchand as an architect. We have him now employed looking after the main post office in the city of Montreal. He is also one of those whose names we are now considering with the view of asking them to be the judges of the plans. It is difficult to find prominent and outstanding individuals in the architectural profession to undertake the duties of judge, as it would deprive them, or their firms, of the opportunity of competing. That is the difficulty, and if we cannot find outstanding architects in Canada who will accept the position of judge, by reason of the fact that they want to compete, it may be necessary to make our selection from the prominent architects in the United States. However, before doing that, the position will be offered to a few of the more prominent architects in Canada, with the view of obtaining suitable men to act.

What has been paid for the site of the new buildings, between the parliamentary grounds and the Perley
Home?

The estimated cost is
something over $2,000,000:	We have paid
out $800,000.

Have the prices in all
cases been agreed upon?
There are a few cases in dispute, not very many.
How far does the site extend to the west?
It goes as far as the Perley Home.
Does it take that in?
Yes.

I? there any new development in connection with the suggestion that Ottawa should become a federal district like Washington? That would get rid of a lot of the difficulties in the way of opening streets that we have been dis cussing to-day.

There has been no development that I have heard of. I am afraid we have been too long in starting. It is a very big question, and, with all that we have had on hand, it has been impossible to give it the consideration which it v deserves. It would involve an enormous expenditure, and a great deal of difficulty. However, it is a suggestion to which a great many people are favourable, and one that is engaging the attention of the Government. It meets with a great deal of favour and I might say with some opposition as well. .

I can assure my hon. friend that the Government will have to come to this some day, and it is just as well to begin to think about it seriously now. Ottawa will be a federal district some day, mark my words. This is the centre of our national government. We shall erect more and more public buildings all over the city, and entanglements between the municipality and the Government as regards taxation will certainly arise. We are practically committed to the beautifying of the city of Ottawa. The appropriation which was voted some years ago extends only for a certain period of years; but my hon. friend knows that we may just as well regard the commission and its work as permanent. Ottawa should be as Washington is, under the control of the Dominion Government. It should be a federal district, and we might just as well face the difficulty, if there be any difficulty, now. Public opinion is prepared for it. Some years ago I heard some objections. It was said that other cities and other provinces would object to it. But the national spirit of this country has not slackened; on the contrary, there is a growing national spirit in Canada, and everybody realizes that Ottawa, being the centre of our national government, should he under the immediate control of the Government. The arrangement has worked admirably in Washington, and I do not see why it should not work well in Ottawa.

Ottawa should have been made a federal district at the time of Confederation. The number of difficulties increase year by year. I am not prepared to say what will happen in regard to this matter, hut it will receive consideration, and it requires a great deal of it.

The reason I put the
question was that a gentleman from Boston who called to see me the other day seemed to have been loaded up with a lot of information about this matter. In fact, he seemed to think it was in definite shape, and was about to he inaugurated practically. I just wanted an official statement.

It would be a good idea af the minister would put on ' Hansard ' the information with respect to the present position of the National Tranconstinental railway, so that the members may at a glance see what the position is. In discussing the subject it would be convenient [DOT]to know the location of each district, and where the spots are that are not completed, and where they are completed.

District A, length, 256 miles, commences at Moncton and runs to the boundary between New Brunswick and Quebec. On this district the grade is totally completed, the tracklaying is completed, the telegraph lines are completed, 98 per cent, of the bridges are completed; the other two per cent of the bridges only require painting, so that the line is practically completed.
District B, length 562 miles. 15 miles of the western end of this district has recently been transferred to District C-D from the New Brunswick and Quebec boundary. Fifteen miles are cut off District C and put on B. The grading is completed for 509 miles, or about 90 per cent, and the tracklaying is completed for 500 miles of the main line and 74 miles of sidings in that district; the telegraph lines have been completed for 357 miles, and the bridges, as on District A, are completed except some painting.
District C-D, length 412 miles, from a point about 204 miles east of Cochrane. The grading is completed for 395 miles. It is between Districts C and B that the only piece of track is not laid from Winnipeg to Moncton, and that applies to about sixty miles. On District C-D the tracklaying is 391 miles of main line and 82 miles of siding; 240 miles of telegraph lines are completed, and the bridges on C are 42 per cent finished, and on D 98 per cent.
District E, length 195 miles, from 204 miles west of Cochrane to 399 miles west of Cochrane, or 125 miles east of Superior Junction. The grading on this division is completed for 158 miles; the track laid on 195 miles of main lines and 17 miles of sidings and yards; telegraph lines completed for 11 miles; bridges 25 per cent completed.
District F, length 376 miles, from 399 miles west of Cochrane, or 125 miles east of Superior Junction, to Water street in Winnipeg. On this section the grading is completed for 376 miles, or 100 per cent. The track is laid for 382 miles of main line, including double track Transcona to Winnipeg, and 132 miles of sidings and yards; telegraph lines 304 miles completed, and bridges 93 per cent completed.
Would the minister add t-o that a statement of the amount of money expended to date, and the estimated amount that will be required to finish the road?
The amount expended up to the 31st December, 1912, was $127,219,863, and the amount I find here estimated for the completion, and which was made up very hurriedly, is $34,087,937.

When is it expected the line will be completed?
Mr. GRAHAM.

We hope that by the end of 1913 the track will all be laid, and the line will be completed to Cochrane this year, anyway, and some time next year to Quebec. That will practically finish the road, and we hope to have the ferry at Quebec going by that time. The contract between Quebec and the New Brunswick boundary will be finished in September next.

What is the situation as to the entrance into Winnipeg from the east? There was an attempted arrangement with the Canadian Northern, by which the Grand Trunk Pacific operated east, Using the Canadian Northern entrance. There was some difficulty as to an entrance from the east into the city of Winnipeg. If I remember correctly, the first location was along the line of the Canadian Northern, but after that the present chief engineer recommended that it be changed to a separate entrance. That matter came up for discussion, and when it came before the Department of Railways, the contention of the chief engineer that there should be an independent entry over a high viaduct was upheld. One of the members of the commission rather favoured the first decision, but the majority, with the chief engineer, favoured the independent entrance.
That has been carried out.	.
It was said to destroy some property of another railway company.

Yes. A settlement has not yet been made in reference to what damage has been done to the Canadian Northern railway. The matter is in the Exchequer Court, but the trial has not taken place yet. The Grand Trunk Pacific railway runs in on the Canadian Northern railway for six miles and the National Transcontinental railway runs in on the east end. I hoped to have those agreements in the House for ratification by Parliament, but I have not got them together yet. I am afraid 1 shall not be able to get them in this session. I think the agreements in regard to the approaches to the terminals should be made for the same length of time, namely 99 years, as the agreement for the terminals made by my hon. friend. The agreements were drawn up at first for 99 years.

Has the hon. minister had an opportunity of considering the question of giving the city of Montreal direct access to the National Transcontinental railway ? Although no distinct promise was made by the late Government to the great commercial metropolis, it was understood by the people that some day", not

too distant, Montreal would be connected with the National Transcontinental. There was no parochial feeling in Montreal more than in Toronto when the project was evolved, and the country in and around Montreal stood for the construction of the Transcontinental. Of course, one cannot eliminate the city of Montreal from direct contact with the Transcontinental. I know that private concerns have obtained at different times charters from the federal Government with the object in view of reaching the Transcontinental from Montreal. The Joliette and Lake Manuan Railway Company was incorporated some years ago, and it appeared at that time that the syndicate which had fathered the scheme was working in conjunction with the -Canadian Northern railway. The Canadian Northern railway has now reached Rawdon, one of the parishes in the county represented by my good friend from Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune). Will the Canadian Northern railway proceed any further ? It has been stated from time to time that some day the road will be extended as far as the Transcontinental. On the other hand, I am informed that the James Bay railway project will, possibly this session or in the near future, obtain from the Government some aid in order to give Montreal direct communication with the Transcontinental. I do not know personally what the Government intends to do, but I am simply voicing the feelings of the people of the district of Montreal. In this I am sure I am supported by my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames): that the commercial metropolis of this Dominion should have, as soon as possible, now that the line is about to be completed, direct access to the whole northern region. This goes without saying. Has my hon. friend a policy on this subject ? Has he come to a decision one way or the other ? Many people in the district of Montreal would like to know if it can be expected tnat the Government will assist the enterprise.

I thoroughly agree
with the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) that there must be a connection between Montreal and the National Transcontinental. That question has occupied 'the attention of the Government for the last two years. The House will remember that last year we voted a subsidy of $d,400 a mile for 500 miles from Montreal to James bay. The company have not been able to finance on that and have been asking the Government for further assistance. I expect to know by Friday what decision we shall come to. It would shorten the distance from- Montreal to Winnipeg by about one hundred and fifty miles by shipping over the Transcontinental line. If we take the Grand Trunk railway or the Canadian Pacific railway to North Bay and T.N.O. then go over to Cochrane, the distance would be about six hundred miles, whereas the distance direct from Montreal to Belle river would only be about three hundred miles. Of course you would have to add the distance from Belle river to Cochrane in order to get the saving.

As this matter is under consideration by the Government at the present time, I want to put in the strongest plea I possibly can for having that road built by the Government as part of the National Transcontinental railway. That road should have access to the two principal ports of the St. Lawrence, Quebec and Montreal. There should be a line from Bell river to Montreal as to Quebec. When the line came down into New Brunswick, it was arranged that both Halifax and St. John should be regarded as the terminal ports for the freight of the National Transcontinental. I do not think the people of Montreal will be satisfied if the line that connects them with the Transcontinental is a privately owned line. Under any system of subsidies that may be given to a private company, it will mean that there will be built an inferior line to the line which the Government itself Is building from Lake Superior Junction to Quebec. We want to feel that Montreal is on a part of the main line of the National Transcontinental and not on a privately owned branch. If, at any time it should be necessary to make alterations in conditions for operating the railway, we should like to feel that the line- that connects Montreal with the Transcontinental is under exactly the same conditions as the line between Quebec and Lake Superior Junction, so that it will not be necessary for us to deal with some private company using what is really an essential part of the main system. 1 sincerely hope that the Government, while they have this matter under consideration, while they have their staff of engineers and the commission and while the plant is in large measure on the spot, will adopt the idea that the line which is to connect Montreal with the Transcontinental is as much a part of the Government built system as any other portion of it, and that it should be carried to completion at the same time as the rest of the road. As it is, the road is to be completed within one or two years and no connection whatever has been as yet provided with Montreal. It seems monstrously absurd that a national transcontinental road, into which $160,000,000 are going is to have no direct connection with the greatest port on the Atlantic coast, namely Montreal. We should have direct connection with the West by this line so that our Montreal freight can go West, and so that freight which is

sent from the West can be brought direct to the port of Montreal when it is profitable to route it that way. To have this great national enterprise completed _ without considering Montreal would, I think, be a fatal error, and I want to put in the strongest possible plea for the construction by the Government of that branch three hundred miles in length from Bell river to Montreal, on the same plans and specifications and operated under the same conditions as the main line.
Did I understand my hon. friend the Minister of Railways to say that the section of the line from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast shall be eojtnt-pleted in 1914?
I think they expect to have it finished next year.
And the line from Winnipeg to Cochrane?
That we expect to finish fully this fall.
And the section from Cochrane to Quebec?
We shall have it running, but not complete; there will be some ballasting and things of that kind to be done.
It will be completed next year?
It will be finished next year, with the exception of the bridge. We expect to have the ferry there next autumn.

That belt of country for one hundred and fifty miles east of Cochrane, most of which is on a level of -only about ten feet above lake Abifibi, is all water soaked, covered with muskeg, a great deal of it covered with low black spruce; and in many places the frost gets into the ground and stays there almost all the year around. A great deal of the under stratum of clay is almost like a glacier, shifting and moving slowly all the time. There are places all along where you find that the embankment has slipped sideways, that the concrete masonry has gone off one hundred feet or so from the road. There is one place at Low Bush river where nine trestles have been built across in succession in the soft mud and they have all gone out and even now they are having the hardest possible work to work through that section. If would certainly seem to me that had a more temporary construction been first built through that section of the road so that there would have been an opportunity, after the trees had been removed and the sunshine could get in, for the land to dry out so that the soil would become more Mr. AMES.
friable, it would have been possible to build embankments that would not sink as they do in many of these muskegs. You will find one place just about the boundary line of Quebec and Ontario, where as fast as they can put in the soil, the earth bulges on both sides and cracks. The only way in which they can lay the tracks is to build three parallel embankments. As often as they keep filling in the middle embankment, and you can put in many hundreds of tons, it sinks and the sides go up. To insist upon keeping up a spirit level grade would be to throw away hundreds of thousands of dol-. lars, and there are a great many places like that in the north country where there must be subsidence grades. Until that country gets dried out and the muskeg is drained and the soil becomes hardened it will be practically useless to keep on increasing the weight of these embankments, because they simply press down in the middle and push out the sides. The time will come when these grades can be filled in, but they can be filled much better and cheaper when ordinary train hauled filling can be brought from a distance, and when the soil gets -dry enough to hold the weight upon it.
The other changes mentioned in that country are through the introduction of momentum grades. It may be necessary at first to have some grades that are even greater than ordinary momentum grades, but what we mean by a momentum grade is a grade between two points, say two miles apart at the same level above the sea, where it is possible for a train to gain enough momentum going down hill to carry it up the hill at the other end of the grade. I contend that the momenturo grade is an accepted prim eiple of engineering used all over the continent. I have here, Willard Beahan's Field Practice of Railway Location, and on page 224 Mr. Beahan writes:
We have seen that the grade to consider is the virtual profile grade. We have seen that without exceeding usual freight train speeds a train will pass down and up in a 25 feet sag with only the usual demand on the locomotives of 7 pounds per ton, i.e., such sags may be operated by the same motive power in the same time and at the same cost as so much straight level track.
That is an accepted' principle of good engineering. The hon. member for Carle-ton, N.B., said that if the engineer, the man who runs the locomotive, would say that, he would accept it more readily.

I did not make any
such statement as that.

Your statement was that
the man who runs the locomotive is the better authority.

There is a railway built
over the Chilian Andes in a .moist difficult country, and an Englishman crossing over that railway not long ago rode on the locomotive and got into conversation with the engineer. He said to the engineer: 'Don't you ever shut her off or use your air?' The engineer replied:	'no, we can just about
stay on the rails in the hollows.' 'Don't you need to take a run at, any of these hills?' the engineer was again asked. 'No,' he replied, 'when she pulls out of a station and strikes her gait, the train pulls just the same way all the way to the next stop.' That is what a train can do over a momentum grade. Let us see what an ordinary momentum grade with a drop of twenty-five feet say in a couple of miles, amounts to. Take a ten-foot billiard table, do you mean to tell me that if there was a drop of a quarter of an inch in the middle of that table a billiard ball would not run down from one end and up the other just as easily as if it were a level table? A drop of twenty-five feet in a couple of miles would be no more than a quarter of an inch drop on a ten-foot billiard table, and a train going at a rate of ten miles an hour would go down a sag of twenty-five feet and come up again without exceeding the usual demand on the locomotive. Let us see what that means in the matter of saving. You can build an embankment fifteen feet across the top, and ten feet in height and that embankment will contain 300 cubic feet to a running foot which at fifty-four cents per cubic yard would cost $6 per lineal foot of track. Calculate that for two miles and you will find what it would cost to make the entire distance a ten-foot high embankment. You can build a line, we will say two miles long with a ten-foot embankment, for $63,360. If it was thirty feet high in the middle it would cost $221,760. In other words there would be by the introduction of a momentum grade a saving of $79,200 per mile. That shows what it is worth to take out some of those absolutely dead levels. I admit that a railway proposition looks very nice indeed if you can see straight ahead for five or ten miles, where there is an absolute spirit level grade all the way. But that is not good railroading, and it is not economical construction. Good railroading is to build a road as cheaply as possible, without interfering with the pulling power of the locomotive. It is perfectly superfluous to make that road absolutely level when you can still maintain the full hauling power of the road by occasionally inserting momentum grades. One of the best authorities in Canada, Mr. Tye, who is president of the Canadian Society of Civil Engineers,
made the following statement in January last in his annual address to that society:
Momentum grades are a great source of saving in cost without increasing the operating expenses. The use of momentum in overcoming short stretches steeper than the ordinary ruling grade is almost always justifiable. The exception is where the traffic is so congested that the possibility of a delay due to the failure of an occasional train to surmount the grade is more important than the undoubted saving in interest charges which they ensure. It will probably be many years before conditions prohibiting their use prevail on any portion of our Canadian railways.
The only exception he makes is that of a road where the traffic is so continuous that the contingency suggested by the hon. member for Carleton might arise, where a train could be stopped it causes delay to the traffic. The probabilities are that it will be many years before there will be so many trains on the Transcontinental that an occasional stoppage will block the traffic. One can see, therefore, what has actuated Commissioner Leonard. As a practical railroad builder, in taking over this road, he saw that money was being wasted for purely artistic purposes. In order that the road might look well money was being spent unnecessarily; and he undertook at once to make a road as it would have been built by any of the great operating companies on the continent of America, and it is to carry out that general principle and, as far as possible, to prevent excessive cost, that this policy has been adopted.

Before the Minister answers, I would like to make a few remarks on the question. Last year,

by the unanimous consent of the House, the estimates went through with a rush, and consequently hon. gentlemen had no opportunity of making any remarks. There was then a vote of $200,000 for the Welland canal, and also a vote of $100,000 for the French river. It was quite evident that neither of those amounts would start the work at either point and, as a consequence, nothing was said, as far as I was concerned, in reference to them. Later, in the summer of 1912, it was announced in the press that it was the intention of the Government to place the Welland canal construction under contract. I happened to see the Prime Minister in Toronto, and in discussing the matter and giving him my opinion of it, he suggested that I should place my views in writing before the Department, because this question had always been a very vexed question on the shores of the Georgian Bay, and the feeling there was that neither work should be carried on until the whole matter had been thoroughly enquired into. I did submit a memorandum on paper in which I do not claim that I set forth any particularly original ideas, I simply placed before the Department the views of the Board of Trade of Montreal, protesting strongly against the deepening of the Welland canal, and I placed on view the opinion of other places as to the French river or Georgian Bay canal. Through the courtesy of the Prime Minister that memorandum was placed before his colleagues. Apparently the view that I took, and in this of course I did not express my own opinion but only opinions culled from very reputable sources throughout the country, apparently had no influence upon them, as is shown by the fact that $2,000,000 were placed in the estimates for the Welland, while only $500,000 is placed in the estimates for the French river enlargement, which will ultimately, I assume, become part of the Georgian Bay canal system. I do not .propose at this late time of the session to make any extended remarks on this question. I believe now, as I have always believed, and as is the opinion of the best business men in the country, that with so many projects before the Government they should have hesitated before engaging on either of these enterprises, and that the whole matter should have been placed before a board of the most eminent engineers that money couicj employ in this country, whether American, Canadian or foreign. However, the Government have taken the matter up and I assume that the Welland canal deepening will now go. on as well as the French river work. In the attitude which I took I was not prompted by any local view, the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway have both invested millions on the

shores of the Georgian bay in establishing huge accommodation for elevators, and have made their railway tracks second to none on the continent. I would stake the opinion of the Canadian Pacific management and the Grand Trunk railway directors against the opinion of any man in this country, and I believe that their plan was the proper plan and the right plan and that neither of these enterprises should have been embarked upon until they had been thoroughly inquired into, especially in view of the facs that Montreal, through its business men and board of trade, more particularly the com section of the board of trade, had protested against the Welland canal work. To-day the country has before it wonderful schemes, schemes that are going to involve millions of dollars. The Welland canal enlargement involves an expenditure of $50,000,000, and the Georgian Bay canal an expenditure of over $100,000,-
000.	The Panama canal is almost completed. Capitalists and the Government are taking steps to attract the trade of the West to Vancouver, believing that a great part of the trade of Alberta will go down m that direction and via the Panama canal to Great Britain. On the other hand, we have this huge expenditure on the Hudson Bay railway I am not going to comment upon that. The Government is committed to it, and it must go on. I simply say that so far as the Welland canal and the Georgian Bay canal are concerned, I enter my protest against either of these projects beinsr embarked upon until the whole transportation question has been placed before one or more of the most eminent engineers in the world.

It is not very often that my hon. friend from Simeoe (Mr. Bennett) and I see eye to eye, but I think his suggestion that there should be full consideration of these great transportation projects before the country is finally committed to them is fair and reasonable. My impression is that so far as the transportation of western grain is concerned, the system whereby the largest vessels on the lakes are used, or can be used, to the fullest advantage, by making a short haul from Fort William to' Midland, with railway transportation from there to Montreal, is the ideal way of getting the crop forward.
And with the Canadian Pacific railway at Port McNichol adjoining.

I mean the Georgian bay
ports which have direct railway communication with Montreal. My impression is that because of the necessity of making as many trips as possible in the short period intervening between the western harvest and the close of navigation, a short route has all the advantages over the long route.
Mr. BENNETT (East Simeoe).
Once the grain reaches the Georgian bay port, then it can be transported by two competing lines of railroad, and possibly three, to Montreal so quickly, that while the theoretical cost may be somewhat larger by this route, we shall say the Midland route, in actual practice, I believe it will be found more beneficial than either the Welland canal route or the Georgian Bay canal route. I am only putting that before the committee as my opinion, and I believe there are good grounds for it. I do not wish to set it up against a well considered opinion that has better evidence behind it. I want the best there is, and I suppose the country is willing to pay for it. It is fair and reasonable to do as my hon. friend suggests, that before the country is absor lutely committed to these two great projects, there should be an investigation of their -merits, a definite decision should be reached, as to what the results are likely to be. This country has a large revenue. We are doing very well, but no country, and no body of people, have money to throw away. We have money to spend on the building of the Georgian Bay canal if that is the best thing to be done, and money to build the Welland canal if that is the best thing to be done, but we have not money to spend on either of these projects unless it is shown that when completed, it is going to be beneficial to the country, and will produce results in proportion to the money expended on them.
