I am not an expert with regard to questions of this kind. All I know is that transportation by water is cheaper than transportation by rail. I heard the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) giving his views on freight rates the other night. I believe myself that railway freights are quite high. I am not an expert and I therefore would not presume to discuss this question in any authoritative way, but I suppose it is in the interest of the railway companies that the rates should be high and it may be that they are high because the railway companies are confronted with the problem of the high cost of living or the high cost of operating. I am not going to enter into that question. What are we considering now? It is not the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. As far as we are concerned on this side of the House we are not in charge of the Government and therefore we cannot do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You did not do it when you could.

What ts the use of my hon. friend reminding the House that we did not do it? It is a plain fact and whether we were right or wrong is not the question to be considered at this moment. But if my hon. friend will be sincere for a moment I will return the compliment by asking him: Why do you not do it now? We had $155,000,000 of revenue while you have pretty nearly $180,000,000. My hon. friend is anxious to send $35,000,000 over to John Bull, who is a money-lender himself; let him put up $35,000,000 to start the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. Were we wrong in not doing it then? Are you right in not doing it now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are going to do it.

If the minister will rise up and say that he will do it I will take my seat right away. Let us be sincere and let us do business in a business way. We had a lecture from a wealthy member from Toronto not very long ago on how to do business in this House. I have been told that the 'hon. Minister of Public Works is a master, not in winning affection, but in winning supporters in this House. I should like the hon. member for North Renfrew to be favoured with the same talent that his master possesses and let him try to convince his master that he should do what he desires. I will pledge him my word that he shall have my full support. We are

passing an item of 'half a million dollars to improve the French river. I do not know much about the French river and I do not like to talk about matters I know nothing about. What I do know about the French river I learned while campaigning once in Nipissing. I know it is in that district. This country is so large that it will take quite a large part of a man's life to study it from Halifax, to Vancouver. Half a million for the improvement of French river! If the Minister of Public Works knew the Riviere des Prairies, commonly known as the Back river, starting at the Lake of Two Mountains and flowing away down to Les Isles de Boucherville at Bout de File, a distance of about thirty miles, he would understand how necessary it is that the work of improving that river already begun should be vigorously carried forward. We have already spent between $40,000 or $50,000 in dredging the river. The channel already dredged is about 100 feet wide and seven or eight feet deep. Dredge No. 6, with a tug, is on its way down to continue the work between the Island of Montreal and lie Jesu. You must not forget that the population of the Island of Montreal and of the lie Jesu is equal to about one-tenth of the population of the whole of the Dominion if we put it at 7,000,000. There are
700,000	.souls in Montreal and the vicinity. What does that mean? That means that the traffic which we have in and around the city is equal practically to one-tenth of the traffic of the whole Dominion.
I am pleased that my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) referred to the transportation of the crop from the West. It is a question, as far as I understand, of speed and cost. Everybody knows that there are not many bushels of wheat, oats and corn shipped from Canada that do not go through the port of Montreal. I know' something about the transportation of grain and I had an opportunity of saying something to this House about it. We can ship grain through the port of Montreal only from May to the last days of November or the first days of December, depending on the condition of the weather. The rest of the shipment of grain goes by Boston, New York, Baltimore, Philadelphia, and Newport News. There was a time when the shipment of our grain was about 'to be transferred to the United States on account of some defects in the inspection system at Montreal. This difficulty was remedied by the Hon. Mr. Bernier when Minister of Inland Revenue, with the result that there is now no complaint about the inspection of grain at that port. Why not spend that half million dollars on Riviere des Prairies and the improvement of navigation around the island of Montreal? We have already started to work. What is the population upon the shores of French river?
Mr. WILSON (Laval).
What port are you going to reach? You will not reach any port on the French river. If it is to please his friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), who is representing that district, _ let the Minister of Public Works say so in order that the committee may be informed of the fact. If the late Government was wise enough, or thought it proper, to start the dredging of Riviere des Prairies in order to improve navigation, the present Government should continue the work because the Back river will be of great use if the Georgian Bay canal project is ever agreed upon and carried out by this Government, and I feel pretty safe in saying that it will be approved by the country at large. Not very long ago I had the honour of being invited by Mr. Poupore, the former member for Pontiac, to attend a delegation which waited on the Hon. Mr. Fielding to whom a petition was presented a mile and a half long containing 60,000 signatures, asking for the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. I approved of the project, as my hon. friend from North Renfrew (Mr. White) approved of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That petition should have been sufficient evidence for Mr. Fielding, then Minister of Finance, to have undertaken the work.

I have listened with a
great deal of attention to the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Wilson), and I can appreciate his interest in the development of the Riviere des Prairies in his own constituency. As evidence of my own interest in the development of that river, I may say that we have in the estimates a vote for that purpose. The hon. member suggests that the $500,000 for the improvement of the French river should be diverted to the improvement of the Riviere des Prairies.	.
Let us cut it in two.

My hon. friend knows that the only request in connection with the Riviere des Prairies is, that a channel nine feet deep should be provided, and he will agree with me that a channel nine feet deep would be of very little service to the transportation of the products of western Canada to the city of Montreal. If the day comes, and when it will come, when we will have the Georgian Bay *canal completed, then the canal will lead to the development of the Riviere des Prairies. I may say that my hon. friend from North Renfrew (Mr. White) has been a most persistent advocate of the construction of the Georgian Bay canal for many years. Personally, I have knowledge of his persistent efforts since I became Minister of Public Works, and I venture to say that no member of this House has taken more of my time than has the hon. gentleman in pressing on me the advantages of the Georgian Bay canal and the necessity for its early construction. The House can well understand that in view of the great difference of opinion which has arisen here, even during the few minutes we have discussed this question, and in view of the fact that I have only been in the Department of Public Works for a short while, I could not reasonably be expected to recommend to my colleagues and to Parliament a sufficient sum of money for the -construction of this great national undertaking as I regard it to be. It is a project that has engaged the attention of former Governments, and of many good citizens in various parts of the Dominion, and it is of special interest to the people of western Canada. We naturally look with care and consideration to any line that will open up a way of transportation for the products of the
prairie provinces; we are prepared to lend our sympathetic and hearty support to any work that will have for its purpose the opening up of additional routes for the transportation of our products. This project received consideration to the extent of an expenditure Of something like $700,000 by the late Government for surveys, upon which to base a recommendation for the carrying out of this great national work. The hon. members for Edmonton (Mr.. Oliver) and East Simooe (Mr. Bennett) seem to have the idea that the most direct and speedy means of transportation would be via Midland and by rail to ocean navigation. Their arguments may be sound, but if this Government and this country are going to rest with confidence upon the fact that one outlet will be sufficient to carry the products of western -Canada to the markets of the world, then I venture to think we will be showing a great deal too much confidence in the railway companies, that they will give such a low rate as would be expected by the growers of grain in the West. With the object of undertaking this great national work, this vast amount of money ha-s been expended by former governments. I am not going to say that it has been expended unwisely. I believe it was a proper expenditure in order that we might be able to ascertain exactly what that great national undertaking would mean to this Dominion. It is to the credit of the Government that preceded us that they appointed a commission to investigate' the possibilities and advantages of the transportation of the products of our people. I cannot do better perhaps than quote the language used in the appointment of that commission and providing the purposes for which the commission was appointed. This is the clause in the Order in Council appointing that commission on the 19th of May, 1903:
The minister apprehends that -in these circumstances it devolves upon -the Dominion Government to consider and -adopt the best possible means of promoting such measures as may enable Canada to control the trans-/ portation of its own products, and it is thought th-at the most efficient method of conducting such inquiry and obtaining the required information is by means of a commission of competent and experienced experts who may be -appointed and authorized under the provisions of chapter 114 of the Revised Statutes of Canada.
My hon. friends at that time suggested Sir William Van Horne, John Bertram and Harold Kennedy. These gentlemen, however, were apparently unable to act. The Government of the day were able t-o secure the services of two men, who, I think were quite competent ito fulfil the important trust that was offered in this connection,

namely: Mr. Ashdown, of the city of Winnipeg, and Mr. Reford, of the city of Montreal. These gentlemen made a very careful study of the question of transportation, and they undertook to deal with the question of the Georgian Bay canal. I think they dealt with it very clearly, plainly and wisely. I would like to read the finding of these gentlemen in respect of the Georgian Bay canal:
Your commission unhesitatingly affirm their belief in the desirability of a through waterway from the head of lake Superior to ocean navigation, to aid in the carriage of the grain and the regulation of rates of a standard not less than that above set forth, so that the largest vessels navigating the great lakes can continue their voyage to ocean navigation or as near thereto as possible. But in view of the fact' that the Government has undertaken the survey of a proposed route by way of the French river to lake Nipiesing, and thence by way of the Ottawa river to Montreal, and as the feasibility of this route from a commercial as well as an engineering point of view, and if feasible its co6t, has not yet been ascertained, and further in view of the fact that the Government has also undertaken the survey of the Welland canal and its vicinity, looking to its possible enlargement and diversion, your commission do not see their way clear to any recommendation as to route, but would recommend that, in case the Ottawa river scheme, because of want of feasibility from a commercial or engineering point of view, or on account of its cost or for other reason be not adopted, then the Welland canal he enlarged and deepened to the standard of the Sault Ste. Marie canal, with a view of enabling vessels of the largest size to continue their voyage to Kingston or Prescott, thus bringing their cargo to within, say 180 miles or less of Montreal before discharging same.

Is it the intention of my hon. friend to spend $500,000 for the improvement of navigation on the French river, or is that done with the view that possibly the Georgian Bay canal can be constructed by that route?

If my hon. friend had
been following me closely in the words which I have just read from the report of
this commission, he would find that the following words have been used:
But in view of the .fact that the Government has undertaken the survey of a proposed route by way of the French river to lake iNipissing, and thence by way of the Ottawa river to Montreal, and as the feasibility of this route from a commercial as well as from an engineering point of view-
My hon. friend will understand from the wording of this report that they recommend the route via the French river, and it is one link in connection with the construction of the Georgian Bay canal?

Is that the opinion of
the hon. minister?
Mr. ROGERS

That is my opinion, and that is why we are undertaking this expenditure of $500,000 in order to carry out the work in the French river portion or link of the Georgian Bay canal, because in that way we hope to develop navigation there that will undoubtedly be useful in many respects. In the first place, we shall be able to develop in connection with that work a water-power in that locality that will in itself be sufficient, in my judgment, to pay the interest upon the amount that will be expended in carrying on the opening up of the French river district.

Where does the hon.
minister propose to sell his power?

My hon. friend surely
understands that there is great development in North Bay, Sudbury and all those growing towns which will all want power. I am sure there will be a ready sale for any power that will be developed along the line of construction of the Georgian Bay canal.
Mr. NESBITT. I know something about the size of those towns and what power they would use. I do not see any possible prospect of paying interest on that investment by bringing power from the French river.

I do not think any power has been developed in any part of Canada that has not found a ready market. I am sure there is no part of the Dominion of Canada that has greater possibilities for rapid development than has that portion of territory to which we are referring. I entirely agree with the course followed by our predecessors in their expenditure in connection with providing a survey of the whole route, including the French river, to the city of Montreal. We have in the department and in the books to which my hon. friend has referred, as full and complete information as any engineers could supply to the people of this country. In so far as the engineering part of the great undertaking is concerned, I regard it as feasible.
The next question that the Government and those responsible must take into consideration is the very interesting suggestion which has been made in the recommendation of this commission which I have just read.
They pointed out to us that it is not only necessary for the Government to ascertain the cost of the work and the extent of its engineering difficulties, but to find out the commercial value of the undertaking. I think it proper that the Government of to-day should follow the recommendation of Mr. Ashdown and Mr. Reford, and. while ascertaining fro mour engineers what the work is likely to cost, and obtaining other information along that line, to make full

inquiry as to the commercial value of this undertaking to the people of the Dominion of Canada. If some hon. gentlemen are of the opinion that the construction of the Georgian bay canal would not be as speedy a means of transportation of the products of our country as would the midland route to Montreal and other ports, such a commission as I am suggesting would inquire into the matter. I find that there is a divided opinion even in eastern Canada in respect to the value of the Georgian Bay canal. I would not be expected, I am sure, by hon. members of this House, in the short period of time during which I have been in office, to recommend an expenditure for the undertaking of this great work in its entirety without the fullest and most complete investigation. As soon as it is possible to get a commission at work to investigate the commercial side of the question, the Government will be in a position to take its stand as to what is best in the interests of the people of Canada in so far as the construction of the Georgian Bay canal is concerned. In the meantime we propose to develop the French river section, and this will, I trust, if it is the recommendation of the commission selected to give the fullest consideration to the commercial aspect of this project, serve the purpose of forming an important part of that grant undertaking the Georgian Bay canal.

What is the minister
going to do with this $500,000 vote?

It is to be used for the
development of the French river section, in connection with the channel.
How wide is the channel to be?
300 feet wide and 22 feet deep.
What is to be the total cost of this work in the French river district?
The estimated cost of the work in the French river section is about $15,000,000.
Is that what is proposed under this vote?

By the expenditure of
this money we hope to make an opening which, with the development of waterpower, will be sufficient to bring in a return to meet the expenditures we are making.

Is there any plan, profile or information of any kind on the table of the House which could be examined by hon. gentlemen and enable them to understand what kind of work will be done under this vote? Does the hon. minister not think that we have enough natural
water-power in this country without dredging a canal for the purpose of producing it?
It seems to me that the sum is quite extravagant. I will admit that proper navigation would be a great benefit to the people living along theshore of that river, but there are no large cities in that district. Is there anv navigation in the French river? What is the average tonnage of the boats plying there, if there are any?

The hon. gentleman is no doubt aware that the reports and books to which he has referred contain certain maps and drawings and complete, data relative to the work to be performed at Montreal and in the French river district, yet he finds fault with the minister because he has not placed any information before us. Complete reports were in the hands of hon. gentlemen of this House during the last Parliament, and full information as to the size of the canal and other paritculans were given in these six volumes. Some members from Montreal are very anxious that this Georgian Bay canal should be built. Whilst we are arguing in this House as to whether we shall have the Welland canal or the Georgian Bay canal, the Government of the State of New York are enlarging the Erie canal. It will be completed within two or three years; it will take all the business now going to Montreal through the Welland canal, and it will take years to build the Georgian Bay canal and bring that business back. To my mind that is a very short-sighted policy. I commend the minister's idea of a transportation commission which will take into consideration the commercial aspect of this whole matter.			.
I commend the minister in his idea of a transportation commission that will take into consideration the commercial aspect of all of these things. Everybody knows 'that the profit earned by the steamers in the lakes traffic is earned on up trip. There is not a dollar made in bringing grain down, practically only the expenses are made; there is no money in the hauling of grain, it is hauled at a loss in order that the ships may have the return package freight cargo. Where does that package freight cargo arise? A certain portion of it in Montreal, possibly ten per cent, but the balance is picked up at other ports on the great lakes going up. There is where the business of the country arises, there is where the large tonnage into the West comes from and every person who has a factory along the line of the great waterway is interested in maintaining and enlarging it so as to get cheaper rates to the West. If that is not done, the European manufacturer, with every advantage of cheap labour, can ship into the West at a

lower price than the people of Ontario. We are confronted with that problem now and it is a .serious one. The Government should consider the enlargement of all waterways, they should consider the advisability not of building the Georgian bay canal, but the building of a. canal that will take the largest ocean, steamers to the head of lake Superior. That is the only possible sensible policy for any government to take. For that reason not only must the Sault canal be deepened-and that is being considered by the United States-to thirty or thirty-five feet, but the new Welland canal must be deepened to the same extent. The Minister of Canals, at a meeting in Ottawa recently stated that it wo<uld have a depth of thirty or thirty-two feet. But the deepening and enlarging of the St. Lawrence canal must also be considered. Competent engineers say, that with a series of five or six dams in the St. Lawrence from Prescott east, a thirty-five-foot waterway may be obtained . clear through from the ocean to Niagara. That is a problem that this country must meet and we must grasp it in order to compete with the new canals in the United States. If we do not, all our work is for nothing.
What will be the depth of the new Erie canal when completed?

I think the new canal
will be about twelve feet, that is for thousand-ton barges. The present canal there is about six feet deep. Some gentleman said that water transportation is the cheapest. The water transportation on the old Erie canal was outdistanced by the railways ten years ago. We must look upon the problem as- broad minded Canadians, and by appointing a commission of big men we can make up our minds what we are going to do. There is no use building small canals that will be forgotten in a few years. Take the Newmarket canal; that was an engineering possibility, the same as the Georgian Bay canal is an engineering possibility. But next comes the question of water and then of tonnage. Before any great undertaking of that kind, of a national character, is started the Government and the people of the country should .be satisfied that it is going to be a commercial possibility and success. The late transportation commission preferred to dwell upon all these works, first as commercial possibilities, not as an engineering possibility. Almost anything is an engineering possibility in these days. The Panama canal is now an accomplished fact. Hon. gentlemen opposite when they were making a treaty a few years aso with the United States, permitted Ambassador Bryce to bring in upon this country one of those beautiful treaties from which Canada derives no benefit, and there was not a word said by Mr. CURRIE.
the late Government in protest. That treaty gave the Americans the free and equal use of the Georgian Bay canal or of any canal that we might build in perpetuity. At the same time why was not the question considered of our being granted in return the free use of the Erie and Panama canals? There is no return to us at all, we do not need any canals that they have On the great lakes, the only works that they could claim anything for was possibly the Livingstone channel and when the survey was made that was found to be one half in Canada. Those questions might have to be considered from the aspect of the benefit of the whole country. Every day we are losing tonnage to the United States. The country that has and controls the channels of transportation is the predominant country of the age. That has been the fact in history. First the Phoenicians, then the Greeks, then ithe Romans, then the Portuguese, then the Spanish and later the British have controlled the transportation of the world- and the greatest current of trade in the world to-day is the current that passes the Detroit river. The American and Canadian tonnase passing that point is about six or seven times the total tonnage of Great Britain or any other country. Our problem as Canadians ought to be to divert that current of trade through our own country so that we shall have the benefit of it and I can assure you that you will not divert that current with any tiwenty-two foot canals, you must have a canal that will meet the situation with ocean vessels and depths. The problem is too large a one for anybody to take a small, local view upon and I ask hon. gentlemen opposite, as well as hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, to forget politics and to assist and commend the department in their efforts to appoint a great big commission on wnich there shall be members of this House, business men and navigators as well as engineers to decide which scheme and which plan is the best for our commerce -and in the interest of the whole country, not for to-day or tomorrow but for the future, some twenty to fifty years hence. Then when we build we will build something that will establish a line of transport that will place the transportation, the trade of the northern half of this continent at the feet of this country. That is the policy I feel like supporting and I think every Canadian will support a policy of this kind. Let us drop all thi'3 endless discussion about building this canal or that canal. Let us do something quickly. If we do not build soon we will lose alii the trade and then we will never recover our lost position.

I want to draw the
attention of the minister and of the House to a phase of this subject which seems to have been entirely forgotten by hon. mem-

bers from Ontario and the West who are discussing this question, and that is the eastern portion -of Canada. In my opinion the eastern portion of Canada is as much interested in the development of one of the great waterways as the West, or more. It is true that the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) treats this question purely from the standpoint of the transportation of grain. From that standpoint, there is, no doubt, a great deal in what he says; and if you have the short water haul from Fort William to the Georgian bay or Midland, the boats can make a greater number of trips during the limited season from the time the crop is ready to move till the close of navigation. But he forgets that there is another side of it and it is the return cargo. In my opinion the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) has really approached this question from the proper standpoint. That hon. member, however, might go very much farther than Montreal or Ontario in connection with the initiation of this package freight." The amount of traffic that would originate east of Montreal would be probably ten times or one hundred times greater than the package freight he has spoken about. At the present time the producers of coal in the maritime provinces are only able economically to land that coal in Montreal. Even with a duty of fifty per cent a ton in their favour they cannot put it up the St. Lawrence river, and the result is that practically all the coal consumed in Ontario is from the United States. If we had waiter transportation, if we could load a vessel at Sydney or any maritime port and bring it right up, I do not care whether it is through the Georgian bay or the Welland and St. Lawrence system, we could get our coal, into the province of Ontario, and instead of buying coal from the United States, the people of Ontario would buy all their coal from the maritime provinces.
At least we will be in a position to compete for the trade. Take the case of our great steel works at Sydney. It is true that with the duty that is now on steel rails, they are able to land their rails in western Canada in competition with the United States, but somebody is paying an enormous amount of freight to get them there. If either of these canals were established, the rails would be practically as cheap at the head of lake Superior as in Montreal, because the extra amount of transportation cost would not be very great. Take many other lines of manufacture. I know manufacturers in eastern Canada who are manufacturing stoves and different classes of hardware, and who are selling them in Vancouver. We cannot sell them to any great extent in the prairie provinces because transportation is against us, but
we can send them round Cape Horn to Vancouver, and do good business, and when the Panama canal is opened we will be able to do better business. But if we had our own water route open, the business of eastern Canada would be doubled, trebled, and I believe quadrupled.
As to the question of which route would be the better, I think the minister has made a very reasonable proposition. 1 understood him to say that he was going to appoint a commission, or at least to take some steps to see which would be the better route commercially. I agree with that. I do not think he is very serious in the expenditure of this half million dollars. If I could form. any opinion from the answers which he gave under the clever cross-examination of my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Wilson), I think it was intended as a sop to my hon. friend from North Renfrew (Mr. White), because that hon. gentleman has been very persistent in asking that something be done. But I do not think that he is devoting that money along the line of carrying out the Georgian Bay project. He wants to do something on the French river, and incidentally to develop some wateT powers. I do not think the Minister of Public Works has actually made up his mind that the work he is going to do on French river is really a commencement of the Georgian Bay canal. As to the question of' whether it should be the Georgian Bay canal or the St. Lawrence route, I agree with the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) that it ought to be one or the other. I do not think there is much justification for the two projects, but the one to he undertaken ought to be so big and broad that it will control the traffic of the northern half of the North American continent. My hon. friend from East Simcoe need not be afraid of any treaties which give the Americans access to our canals. The more American traffic we get into our canals and ports the better for the people of this country. I would like to see every bit of traffic which comes from Chicago diverted to Canadian channels. It would make business at our ports, in our shipping, and for our transportation companies. I am not in a position to offeT an. opinion as to which is ihe better route. There was a time when I was very much impressed with the possibilities of the Georgian Bay canal, but looking at the question from the point of view of the man in the street, I think the route which ought to be developed is the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence route. I admit that there is not much use in developing the Welland canal unless we deepen and develop the St. Lawrence as well. I believe there is enough water power to be

developed from Prescott to Montreal to pay the interest on the whole proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will that power not be international?

Not very much of it.
The power at the Long Sault would be international, but from that point down it is all Canadian. However, that does not make any difference to me. I am a free trader to some extent, though not altogether, and I would just as lief sell power as sell wheat. If we have water-power that we do not want to use ourselves and the American people want it, and are willing to pay for it, I do not see why we should not sell it, so long as we keep control.
Suppose you get $10,000,000 or $15,000,000 a year for it?

Of course, I would have all proper precautions. Our own people must have the first chance at it. Outside of transportation there is nothing so valuable to any nation as cheap power, and if you can give the manufacturing industries powrer at $10 or $12 per horse-power, you will do more to build up manufacturing than all the tariffs you can throw about it. The St. Lawrence route has a great advantage over the other in that it develops an enormous amount of power right in territory where there are millions of people to-day, and where industries are established, and will be established one hundredfold in the years to come. You will get great water-powers on the Georgian Bay route, but it has not as yet any great centres of population. But that is a matter which it would be the duty of the commission to investigate and report upon. I hope the minister will go on with one or other of these routes, and that he will make it so big and broad and deep that it will not only carry our own business eastward, but the great bulk of American business as well, and that it will -give us a chance in the maritime provinces to send our products westward. It will help us and help the people of Ontario, and what helps the people of Ontario and of the maritime provinces must help the people of Canada as a whole.

I endeavoured to get an answer from the minister as to what he intended to do with this $500,000. He said he wanted to develop the French river. He said that the canal would be 300 feet wide, and 23 feet deep. How far could he go with $500,000 under these conditions? I do not believe he could go further than the length of one of these desks. He intends either to develop power, or to start the Georgian Bay canal, and I would like to know which. If he intends to develop power, and he has a market for power in that country, which I doubt, I have no Mr. CARVELL.
objection. He knows it will require some-development on French river to run a boat.
Does my hon. friend not know that the French river in many places is nearly half a mile wide and forty or fifty feet deep?

But there are spots
where it is not very deep. They have even to build slides in places to run down the logs. I have no objection personally to my hon. friend developing power on the French river, but if he is spending this money with the object of making a canal out of French river, then I am absolutely opposed to it. They talk about it costing $100,000,000. It will cost $200,000,000 or $250,000,000 to build any canal by way of the French river to Montreal. If there is to be a -canal, I am very strongly in favour of the Welland canal route. I quite agree with my hon. friend from East Simcoe that the question-should be thoroughly investigated, but I understand that the late Government did thoroughly investigate the question of the Welland canal, that they spent a certain-amount of money in borings and in investigation. I also understood that the present Government did the same thing last year, so that we ought to be in a pretty good position to know what the cost is likely to be,, and whether it is a feasible proposition commercially.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does
my hon. friend think that the report which was submitted in connection with the Georgian Bay canal route, and which has been referred to by the hon. member for Laval is not correct? My hon. friend says that it will cost $200,000,000 or $250,000,000. The report of the commission is to the effect that it will cost $100,000,000 in round figures. Evidently my hon. friend does not think that the report is correct.
I think that they have underestimated the cost by fifty per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend ever
been over the route?
Yes, most of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What part?
Nearly all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Was he ever at Pembroke?

Yes, I have been at Pembroke. You have to go there in daylight to find the town. I absolutely agree with the minister when he says that this question should be thoroughly investigated by the most capable men that he -can get and not men appointed from a political standpoint. I do not mean to say that he cannot get just as capable men who are Conservatives as any other kind, but political considerations ought not to have any weight in the appointment of such a commission of

investigation. They should be a commission of the most capable engineers and, as the hon. member for North Simcoe says, business men, because it is the business aspect of the question that is going to be looked into. I believe that the undertaking from the engineering aspect, is possible but not probable. But it should be inquired into from a commercial standpoint because it is from that point of view that we have to look at all these public questions. I was sorry I was not here the other night when the Hudson Bay item went through, because I would like to say that I am amongst those who do not believe in the Hudson Bay railway at all.
You are too late.

I know it is too late, and I know that we on this side of the House are just as much committed to the project as hon. gentlemen on the other side. I think both parties are absolutely wrong in giving their approval to this undertaking. Referring again to the Georgian Bay canal, I hope that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works will appoint a commission which is capable of advising him with regard to this question before he goes into the undertaking. I think that to spend this money on the French river route with the object of favouring somebody politically is a great mistake, and a cruelty to the people of the country unless it can be carried out from a commercial standpoint, as I do not believe it can. As to the Welland canal, I think it can be successfully carried out from the commercial point of view, and I think it ought to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have an extract here from Washington which I think it would be well to place on ' Hansard.' It is as follows:
Washington, D.C., May 5.-Legislative action on the resolution to enter into negotiations with the Dominion of Canada or Greac Britain regarding a better waterway through the Great Lakes is promised to-night, following a conference between Senator Stone, of Mississipi, and Senator Townsend, of Michigan. This resolution will undoubtedly be favourably reported from the Foreign Relations Committee, of which Senator S'one is chairman.
Senator Townsend's idea is to open up the passageways between tlie Great Lakes, and to improve the harbours to such an extent that ocean going vessels will be able to dock at Duluth, Minnesota, and all other lake ports.
From Duluth to Liverpool would be the trans-Atlantic route under the Townsend idea. He believes that unless the United States takes the initiative in this matter the Canadian Government will dig a canal from the Georgian bay to the Ottawa river and provide practically the same accommodations for trans-Atlantic steamers with the advantage to the Dominion of controlling the artificial waterway entirely.	*
Evidently our friends to the south of us are afraid that we may do so.
Well, he has got a lot of thinks coming to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Senator Townsend's scheme includes the widening and deepening of the Welland canal and the improvement of waterways from Montreal to Lawrenceburg. The wording of his resolution is short and simple, and reads:
' Resolved, that the President be requested to enter upon negotiations with Great Britain or the Dominion of Canada with a view to an international agreement for the concur-, rent or co-operative improvement of navigation in waterways used, or which can be used, as common for the commerce of Canada and the United States.
This was introduced at one time as a proposed amendment to the Reciprocity Act. It! was introduced again as it now stands, but the Committee on Foreign Relations took no action upon it. It is again before Congress; with the promise from 'Senator Stone that it will be acted upon and a favourable report from the committee is a little more than possible.	t
If our friends to the south are so anxious for the deepening of the Welland canal, they ought to provide half of the cost.

To come back to the
item, I suppose that probably when we come to the item of the Minister of Railways and Canals of $2,000,000 for the Welland canal we will have the discussion-*
Over again.
There will be an opportunity for discussion. As to the item for the French river, if we vote this we are committed to an expenditure of $15,000,000.
Not necessarily.
That is what I understood.

My hon. friend says
' Not necessarily.' What can we do with $500,000 if this is not the beginning of a work which will cost $15,000,000 in all to obtain a deeper navigation of the French river and through Lake Nipissing to North bay? If we spend that $500,000 what do we get?

W'e may use some of it in the construction of a dam where Lake Nipissing empties into the French river, and thereby save a great deal of dredging. We have already done some work there and we may require more if we do nothing else.

It is quite important that the committee should understand what we are doing with the vote of $500,000. If we are committed to $15,000,000, then the Georgian Bay canal is started.
1X171

You would not expect
us to undertake to commit ourselves to the whole project without having the report of a commercial commission, as suggested by the commission which recommended the work, and I think it is very sound judgment on their part, I entirely approve of it and I propose to appoint this commission at once and have a report on the commercial value of the undertaking.
We want a plain statement of what we are doing. The Government is not announcing a policy of constructing the Georgian Bay canal by this vote?
Not yet.

It is asking for $500,000 to Start work that will cost, when completed as far as North Bay, $15,000,000 and, if we are committed to an expenditure of $15,000,000, then the Georgian Bay canal is started and will be completed, because the Government would scarcely ask for $15,000,000, which would probably be $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 before that particular work would be completed to North Bay, without the larger project in view. Then I think we can take it for granted that this $500,000 is merely for a preliminary skirmish on the French river for the building of a dam and incidentally the developing of some water power. Do we understand that the country is not committed to an expenditure of $15,000,000 for the opening up of a channel to North Bay, and the construction of docks and so on- and that the Government is not announcing a policy of construction, or beginning the construction, of the Georgian Bay canal and will not do so until such time as it appoints a commission to investigate the question from the commercial standpoint and until it gets its report?
That is about right.

No matter what happens to the Georgian Bay canal or the "Welland canal, the French river portion of the canal would give an outlet for the products of the clay belt of New Ontario, in which in the future millions of bushels of all kinds of grain will be grown. In any event, the money expended here will not be lost.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say the wheat would be brought from the clay belt to North Bay and then shipped by water down the Welland canal?

The mining operations in that northern country will require large quantities of coal, and that coal will be brought to North Bay from Lake Erie. I am looking at this from a commercial and not a political standpoint. When the coal
' Mr. GRAHAM
vessels unload at North Bay, they must get return cargo, and what more natural than that return cargo should be wheat.
If I want to go to the Chateau Laurier, do you think it would be a good thing for me to go around by the Union station ?
It is not the same thing at all.

Last year when Mr. Monk was Minister of Public Works, we endeavoured to obtain some information as to the policy of the Government with reference to the Georgian Bay canal, and we failed. One evening last session Mr. Monk was not in the House and the estimates were taken charge of by the hon. Postmaster General, who, I am bound to say, contrary to his usual practice, gave somewhat evasive replies to the questions put him. The best I could get out of him was that there was an amount somewhere in the estimates which would be expended during the then coming year, in obtaining information about the Georgian Bay canal project. I will ask the Minister of Public Works to-night to enlighten us with regard ro that statement made by one of his colleagues last session. As I understand the declaration of policy made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Rogers) to-night, on behalf of the Government, the Welland canal project is to be proceeded with and the Georgian Bay canal project is not, although the French river improvement is to be undertaken. We have a natural curiosity to know how this $500,000 is to be expended, and . I know the minister sufficiently well to believe that he would not ask. us to vote $500,000 without giving us details as to the manner in which it is to be expended. We cannot be expected to take a leap in the dark when a very much larger sum than $500,000 is apparently ultimately involved.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say ihat this project, if carried to completion, would involve the expenditure of about $15,000,000, and that by voting this item _we were committing ourselves to the carrying out of the scheme in its entirety. I now ask the minister to enlighten the committee as to that and also as to the expenditure of the money, which we were informed by one of his colleagues last year had been voted for the purpose of getting information regarding the construction of the Georgian Bay canal.

I have no doubt that had my predecessor remained in office he probably would have carried out what had been promised on his behalf by the Postmaster General, and he would be prepared to-night to give the information the hon. gentleman

(Mr. Murphy) has referred to. Since I took charge of the department, I am free to confess I have not had time to give this matter the consideration its importance deserves. We ask for this $500,000 in order that we may be in a position to get full and complete information, so far as the French river is concerned, during the coming year. I understand that with this vote a considerable amount of valuable work can be done, which would save a large amount of money in connection with the dredging of lake Nipissing, and that it would develop a certain amount of waterpower, which will be, in itself, very valuable. While there may be some indefiite-ness about that, I can assure my hon. friends that the money will be expended in the public interest and care taken that value is received for every dollar of it. I believe it will be expended in such a way as will prove satisfactory to the members of this House and to the people of the country.

While we may be willing to accept the statement of the Minister of Public Works that this money will be expended in the public interest, yet we are entitled to information as to how it is to be expended. Is it going to be expended on the construction of a dam, as the minister would seem to suggest ? The impression the minister leaves on me tonight- is that he has not decided on anything as yet, and that if the money is voted he will have it there to do with it whatever may -come handy later on. We should not be asked to vote money under such circumstances.
The chief engineer says this amount will be required in connection [DOT] with the carrying on of the project.
Was not all that information obtained under thb late Government ?
The chief engineer says the information was obtained, but only in a very general way, and not in a way that would be sufficient to warrant the undertaking of definite and -specific works.
How much money has been expended altogether in obtaining information about this Georgian Bay canal ?

Something like $700,000
for the whole four hundred and forty miles.
The Georgian Bay canal has been surveyed inch after inch and foot after foot, and the minister must know what are the conditions of that river. We are entitled to have detailed information.

This money is to be expended to get the detailed information
which the hon. gentleman wishes to have. We have the general information in the report of the engineer, to which my hon. friend has referred, but we have not the detailed information necessary when we come to make plans and specifications for a project which will require the expenditure of a great deal of money. Before any minister would recommend to this House the expenditure of such a large sum of money, he will have to be in possession of the detailed information which we can secure by this expenditure.

Would this be some explanation? The Minister of Railways represents that constituency and is committed to placing in the estimates $2,000,000 for the Welland canal. Therefore something must be done 'to appease the wrath of his own electors who are expecting the Georgian Bay canal to start right away.

I never heard anything
about that.

This $500,000 is to get information, plans and specifications and general improvements, but for what? If it were part of the Georgian bay canal scheme and the policy were so announced, I would understand why this money is required. The Minister of Public Works says:	No; if we ever build the Georgian
Bay canal, this will be for the work on it, but we are not going to commit ourselves to it until we make further investigations. Therefore this money cannot be for working plans and specifications for the development of that great scheme. The Minister of Public Works must be going to do some thing practical on the French River; otherwise this money must be to please the Minister of Railways. If the money is to do any work on the Georgian Bay canal, the minister ought to be able to tell us what he is going to do with it.

That will all depend on the report of the commission which will be appointed very shortly. If they report favourably on the undertaking, it would be a mistake to lose a year, and we should have sufficient money in the estimates to enable us to get complete plans and details, in order that we may present at the next session of Parliament a proper report as to the undertaking.

My hon. friend says that he is not going to go on with the expenditure of this money until he gets the report of this commission, but he does not want to lose a year. He will get their report and act on it before he lays it before Parliament. Is that what the vote is for?

We will have the work
extended, because we believe that the work

on the French river section itsell will be of great value to the locality and to the country as a whole. We want plans and reports on that work.

$100,000 was voted last
session. Was any of it expended?
Nothing was expended.

The hon. minister says
that all he proposes to do is to take this $500,000 in order to get the commission to work, and that when he receives their report, he will act on it. .1 do not think the minister, in all seriousness, will tell the House, after the reports that have been made for the past few years on the Georgian Bay canal scheme, and after an expenditure of three quarters of a million in order to get these reports, that the section of the French river up tc North Bay is not as well known by the reports already received as anything possibly could be. It does not require $500,000 more to get further reports in order that the work may be gone on with. I am not in favour of the Georgian Bay canal scheme, because I do not believe that at the present time, with boats of'a maximum length of about 700 feet, you will ever get the carrying trade to go through the Georgian Bay canal. If so, you are better off with the deepening of the Welland canal, and the people of Canada will be saved the amount of money which would be spent on the Georgian Bay canal. The prospective expenditure is'$100,000,000. If you consider what has been expended in this and other countries on works of similar enormous proportions, you will find that not a hundred million will be expended on the Georgian Bay canal, but about $300,000,000 before it is completed. One reason given why the Georgian Bay canal should be constructed is that between Duluth and Port Arthur it will save two days coming and two days going. I think the report brought down last year made that statement. I do not believe that is so, for this reason. Even if the Georgian Bay canal is constructed, with the number of locks that will have to be made on it, and with the maximum length of boats of 700 feet, you will find that boats of that capacity will take the route of the Welland canal rather than the Georgian Bay canal. If boats are to go through the Georgian Bay canal, they will have to be smaller, and consequently the expense for carrying grain will be greater. After the Georgian Bay canal is constructed, you will find that boats will still go through the Welland canal; and that the Georgian Bay canal, except that through its construction certain water powers will be developed in that country, will be of absolutely no use. I believe, with the reports we have to-day, that we have all the infor-Mr. ROGERS.	-
mation necessary, and that this expenditure of $500,000 is practically money thrown away. If it is to cost $500,000 to know whether or not the Georgian Bay canal is feasible from the mouth of the French river up to North Bay, heaven only knows what the Georgian Bay canal will cost from the French river to Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There
seems to be a considerable difference of opinion on the other side of the House with regard to the Georgian Bay canal project. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) and the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) have contended that, notwithstanding the fact that the late Government expended some $700,000 on surveys, these surveys were practically usele-ss.

I do not propose to have that interpretation put upon my words. I said that the expenditure of $700,000, with the reports and papers that were brought down, had given us all the information necessary to enable us to make up our minds with regard to the construction of this canal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The report which these
engineers brought down was to the effect that this project would cost in the neighbourhood of $100,000,000.
Which I do not believe.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then the money was uselessly expended, so far as hon. gentlemen opposite are concerned. I am sorry the hon. member for South Renfrew is not in the House, because I wanted to ask him whether he is in favour of the Georgian Bay canal or the deepening of the Welland* 'canal, and which project he thinks the Government of this country should undertake at the present time.

I think the hon. member for West Lambton supplied a good Teason why this item should be passed to-night. 'He has pointed out that we have already spent $700,000 on surveys; that we have in the department, the reports regarding those surveys, and that he does not believe a word of what the engineers say in regard to 'the matter.
I did not say that.

When a commission ts
appointed to inquire into the commercial aspect of this matter, and when they read the assertion of my hon. friend to the effect that he does not believe the report of the engineers appointed by the Government which he supported, it will be a great question for the commission to decide as between my hon. friend and the engineefs. They might 'be able to reeom-

mend the construction of the canal as a commercial undertaking if it were to cost $100,000,000, and might refuse to recommend it if it were to cost $300,000,000. I think, therefore, that we are justified in having plans and specifications made with regard to any particular section to which we are giving consideration. The chief engineer informs me that, while we have had the survey to which my hon: friend refers, we have not, in the department, that specific information as to detail work that would enable us to be definite as to the actual cost.
The minister, then, will acknowledge that this $500,000 is for the appointment of a commission to report on the section between the mouth of French riveT and North Bay.
This whole amount does not necessarily go to them.

The use to which this
money is to be put seems to change each time my hon. friend deals with it. I would suggest the wording of the item should be changed so that it will specify that it is for the purpose of collecting information.
Quebec harbour-dry-dock at Lauzon,

Who are the engineers?

Mr. Swan, Mr. Wilson
and Mr. Laflenr.

What was the price
paid for the site?

When my hon. friend comes back with his estimates to-morrow, I would like him to give me the names of the owpers of the site, and the amounts which are to be paid to each of them. What is the total estimated cost of the dry-dock?

not be possible to say now what the cost will be.

What will be the size
of the dock?
1,150 feet long by 125 feet wide.

What is the location,

At Levis, right close to
the old dock.

thinks that there will be work for both.

cents a square foot would come to $70,000.

At five cents a foot it
would be $70,000.

I understand that
$70,000 will be the price paid for the site?
_ Mr. ROGERS:	The engineer says that
is the estimated value. The land is being expropriated, and we expect to be able to secure it at that price.

I raise no objection
to the construction of the dock, but as to the price my hon. friend may rest assured that five cents a foot in Lauzon is a good rate, and if the parties will not accept that figure, if the minister resorts to expropriation I am inclined to think the Government will win.
We will go to the Exchequer Court, we are not going to decide it.

When is it expected the
dock will be finished?

About two years after
the letting of the contract. We will probably let the contract within the next two months.

How does that dock
compare with other docks?

It is one of the largest
in the world.
Red river, St. Andrews lock and dam, construction of approach, $70,000.

This has been a hardy
recurring annual for many years. What particular work is this estimate for?

The work on the St. Andrew's lock is certainly one that we are all proud of up there. This is necessary in connection with the construction of approaches to complete the work; this is for approaches to the bridge over the dam.

The construction of the
lock and dam at St. Andrews has created



dead waters for a number of miles up and down the river in front of the city of Winnipeg, which has had a certain injurious effect in regard to sanitation. Is there any proposal whereby that situation can be relieved in any way?

I understand there has
been some difficulty in that [DOT] connection, but I have not heard of it as being very serious up to date. I understand that matter will be looked into by a committee appointed by this House. The raising of the water has done a great deal of good in other respects.
Perhaps the hon. member for Selkirk could give some information?

This is, of course, a big question, but, as far as the dam is concerned, there is no means of relieving the situation; the remedy is for Winnipeg to stop putting raw sewage into the water. That is the only remedy, and I think the people of Winnipeg realize that fact. The "'building of the dock has created a large body of dead water, but it has also accomplished a great work, and has made possible navigation from the head of lake Winnipeg to the city of Winnipeg. The approaches to the bridge are necessary. It will be remembered that the bridge was placed across the dam in such a way that it was of no use without approaches. The committee to which my hon. friend refers is not charged with any responsibility in regard to this situation of the city of Winnipeg particularly. It would be well for the Public Works Department to take cognizance of the conditions as they are, and to see what relief can be provided, because I am strongly impressed with the view that the conditions there are apt to be very serious. I would suggest that something might be done to relieve the situation by giving notice that at certain times the water would be allowed to run off.
Every fall the sluice gates are raised and the water is lowered some twenty feet, and a great deal of the sewage is run off.

Everybody who lives in
that part of the country knows that the condition of health is dangerous towards the fall. A serious condition of affairs has been created by that time, the damage has been done.

I do not think that
anything done, so far as the lock or dam is concerned, would relieve the situation Mr. OLIVEP
to any great extent. The real and only cure would be to stop the putting of sewage into the Red river.
Vancouver harbour improvements, $500,000

This is in connection
with the wharf started some time ago and just completed.

It will be made by us.

This is part of the cost of a new building that we propose erecting as a post office at Amherst.

What is
wrong with the present building?

Last year an item of
$5,000 I think was placed in the estimates for ithe purpose of building an addition to the present public building. 11,000 and at the present rate of growth there will be 20,000 bv 1920.

I would like to express my regret on behalf of the people of Yarmouth that there is nothing in the main or supplementary estimates for improvements on the Yarmouth public building. The report that we have from the customs officials is that we have constant, almost hourly, complaints in regard to the present location of the customs house. Mr. Chairman, when Mr. Dugas, now one of the judges of our courts, was a member for the county of Montcalm, he succeeded, after repeated efforts to obtain a post office for the parish of St. Jacques de l'Achigan. That parish is very important in all respects.

In 1909, when I was elected as representative of that county, I repeated what Mr. Dugas had said and a sum of $15,000 was put in the estimates for the construction of a post office in that parish. It was my misfortune to he elected as a Liberal, and I see now that the amount has vanished from the estimates. I have repeatedly asked the former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) to put that sum back in the estimates, but he has always turned a deaf ear, saying: 'We shall see later on; we will consider the matter;' and he is still considering it. Meanwhile the post office is not being built.
St. Jacques is an old parish with a large agricultural population. A bank has been established there; a huge convent, a model school and various industries are to be seen in that place. There is a large tobacco factory; and it was for that reason that a post office had been granted to the parish.
Since the new administration came into power, the amount put in the estimates in favour of St. Jacques has been taken off, and the former Minister of Public Works gave it to his own county after taking it away from the county of Montcalm. And this is'called ' British 'fair play.' Woe begone fair play, I think. It seems to me that, the new administration was bound in honour to carry out the decisions taken by the former administration. I would like to know by virtue of what principle they have acted.
The land had been bought, and the work of building was about to begin when the Nationalist leader, Mr. Monk, decided to commit this injustice towards the ratepayers of St. Jacques, by cutting off this vote of $15,000.	^
I can understand the Government taking revenge by beheading employees who meddle in politics, but a post office is never guilty of such a crime. Why, then, should that amount be struck off the estimates? Now, when I ask that the amount be put back in the estimates, the answer is: ' We shall see to it,' but nothing is done. The buying of a site shows that it was the intention to build that post office, the construction of which has been put off till this day, and is still being put off.
I ask the hon. Minister of Public Works what the Government intend to do? When a former administration have decided upon a certain thing, I say that the new Government which succeeds them have no right to ignore their decision and to take the amount to give it somewhere else. The engagement should be carried out, whether the members are Conservatives or Liberals. The Government should keep the pledge taken by the former administration and do justice to the electors I have the honour to represent here.
The 35 millions you have voted for the navy you will not have the opportunity to spend. Give them for post offices as necessary as that of St. Jacques, and thus give justice to those electors who claim their share of protection and the share of sunlight to which they are entitled. Give a little of that public money to the fine county of Montcalm.

I wish to give my hearty support to what has been expressed by the hon. member for Bonaventure, and the hon. member for Montcalm. The county of Bonaventure is one of the largest in the province of Quebec, it ranks second in area and it has not been very much endowed with the good things of this world. Its population is poor but it pays its share of taxation, and it seems to me that the Government should have at least implemented not only the promise, but the item which had been in the estimates under the preceding Administration. The county of Bonaventure, as my hon. friend knows, is settled by the old United Empire Loyalists and by the Acadians, and it has been worthily represented in this House by my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil). It seems to me that it is rank injustice to deprive that county' of what it had expected from the Government. As regards Montcalm, it is probably the most prosperous farming county in the province of Quebec. One parish, St. Jacques, is certainly the richest parish in the province. In that parish the farmers have succeeded in establishing the tobacco industry on a large scale. Splendid farms can be seen throughout that parish and throughout the constituency. When this amount was put in the estimates I think I was a party to it; the site was selected and paid for, plans prepared and I think the old building demolished. Is it not strange that the amount has been removed from the estimates just as my hon. friend came into the Department of Public Works? I could understand perhaps the late Minister of Public Works, Mr. Monk, wiping out the item. He has been very prominent in the political battles of our province and probably has received some hard knocks from the hon. member from Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune), and my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), but my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has not been so prominent in our province and surely he would not have taken it upon himself to deprive those two constituencies of their due on account of any personal attacks that might have been made by the two members. I would ask him to be fair and just towards these two constituencies. We all know that our friend is the power behind the throne, that he has all authority and that by a wave of his hand he could reinstate the two items in the estimates. I can assure him he will

win favour by it and the people will be very grateful. It is a rank injustice to deprive the two counties of their buildings.

I think it is hardly fair

The late Administration undertook to give the eastern section of Montreal a post office which is situated in the St. Mary's division. Five or six years ago an inspection was made by the postal authorities, in conjunction with the Public Works Department officers, and a selection was made in the constituency represented by my hon. friend. The building is a credit to the Government, to the city of Montreal, and also to my hon. friend, because he had a lot of trouble in obtaining it from the late Administration. I now wish to put in a word for the St. James' division. As the minister knows, the city of Montreal is increasing by leaps and bounds. It will soon have a population of
700,000.	There is a post office at Maison-neuve, one at Hochelaga, which is one of the wards of the city, and one at St. Mary's. These are all for the east, and cover a very large area. Then there is the thickly settled St. James division, which is the wealthiest section of Montreal east. The population has been increasing considerably there, and out of the old ward of St. James have been carved several municipal divisions of the city of Montreal. Influential people belonging to both political parties have been petitioning the Government to obtain a postal station. While the postal station was being erected in St. Mary's we decided to have a postal station on Amherst St. It was fully equipped, from a postal point of view, but when the pew office in. St. Mary's was opened, orders *came from Ottawa to close the Amherst St. postal station. There has been such a hue and cry about it that the Post Office Department has been compelled to reopen that .postal station, but it is not sufficient for the needs of the district- You will have to -build in St. James division a postal station
such as you have built in St. Mary's. The people of St. James will not go to St. Mary's because i't is too far away, and they have to go' as far as the central post office in Montreal, which is also quite a distance away, or past Bleury st. On St. Catherine st. west of Peel st. you have three or four postal stations, and you are contemplating the erection of new iones. I think it is only fair that the largest and wealthiest division in the eastern part of the city of Montreal should be provided with a postal station. To-day the idea is not so much to get large post offices in large cities. There is a central office, but in order to distribute the work more economically and more rapidly, the prevailing principle in post office matters is to erect stations in the suburbs. I would ask my hon. friend to attend to this, and to give the people of Montreal east what they deserve to have. The municipal council of Montreal, the citizens, irrespective of party politics, and the postal authorities of Montreal are all in favour of this. We made a great mistake some years ago in providing Only for the alteration of the general post office in Montreal. My hon. friend will remember that we had a building on St. James street, next to the Bank of Montreal, and we decided to purchase the Gazette building. We thought at that time that it would be adequate for the needs of the city for many years to come. The highest postal authority in Montreal is Mr. Gaboury, the new superintendent, and he states that already the central office, with these additions, is too small and that it is being congested through the invasion of other public departments in Montreal. I see that, for instance, the marine agency in Montreal has been removed from the Boyer block in Commissioners street to the central post office. The marine agency of Montreal is quite an institution, and as the trade of the port of Montreal increases, it will take more space each year- and it will congest more and more the post office. The policy in every large city, not only on this continent, but in Europe, is to distribute postal work among different sub-stations. I hope that my hon. friend will see that St. James division, which is the wealthiest and most important in the eastern section of Montre 1, is provided with a postal station.

I fully concur in the remarks which the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has just made. He has clearly put the situation before the House. St. Jarne-s Division is a more or less commercial division, St. Catherine street, which is the main commercial street, running through the entire length of the division. An available mail service is a necessity for the division. For some time we have had a temporary mail service on

Amherst street. The hon. Postmaster General has thought fit to close that temporary office. On a question I put to him in this House, he answered that he would immediately re-open that office, adding that he would only re-open it temporarily because he had under consideration the establishment of a general post office for the St. James Division.
I must say furthermore that there is quite a distance between the post office on Plessis tstreet, near St. Catherine street, and the post office on West St. Catherine street, near the University.
The Government will understand- especially the Postmaster General who knows Montreal perfectly well-and will see the necessity of building in the centre of the city, near St. Denis street-which is the division line 'between St. James and St. Lawrence Divisions-a post office to accommodate that division.	_
To corroborate what I have just said, allow me to quote what was said by Mr. L. G. Gaboury, post office inspector, in an interview reported in La Patrie, April 25, ,1913. He made statements which seem to be very reassuring:
We now have, said he, five offices where ithe complete service is carried on ithe same as it is in the main office on iSt. James street. These offices are: postal station B, west St. Catherine street; station C, Amherst street, which -will soon toe replaced toy the office on Plessis street, now toeing ibuilt; station D, Centre street, and station E at 'the .Mile End Of the service in the eastern pant, compared with the western part, he went on to say, I would rather not say anything, but I will let you know that I have transmitted to the department a report, the complaints which have appeared within the last few days in several of the Montreal newspapers.
As to the rumour according to which the Government intends to dose station B, when the new "building at tbe corner of Bishop street, shall be completed, Mr. Gaboury denies it altogether. On the contrary, the Government will enlarge that station to meet the desires of the traders in that part of the city, who have forwarded to the department numerous and pressing requests. In fact, said Mr. Gaboury, station B is rendering invaluable services and contributing highly to the general efficiency of the postal organization. Thus, in only one day no less than 3.000 persons coming to the different wickets have been counted. (Nothing could show the esefulness of that office better than the crowd which is constantly oocdng to it. lit would.be most unfair to expect these clients, the majority of whom are business men, should be compelled to go to the St. James street office, which besides, is hardly sufficient to accommodate the central part of the city.
I must say that for some time past a somewhat violent dispute has arisen in the press about this post office. But leaving aside that violent language, all are agreed on the necessity of having a new post office Mr. LAPOINTE (iSt. James, Montreal).
within the limits I have just indicated. So true is this t/hat Mr. Gadboury continues to tell us so while making a comparison of the post offices, which rumour had it, were intended to he closed. I have nothing more to add except to thank the Postmaster General for having immediately, at my request, re-opened the post office on Amherst street, and if I understand his words, such as reported in the ' Hansard,' the re-opening of that office has only been made temporarily until something permanent is done.

I would like to direct the attention of the hon. gentleman who leads the House to the fact that there are two or three important Bills standing in the name of the Postmaster General. I have not seen the Postmaster General in his seat for several days; I was informed that he had resigned, but perhaps my hon. friend can inform me as to that, and whether it is the intention of the Government to proceed with the Parcel Post Bill, the Wireless Telegraph Bill and the Letter Carriers' Salaries Bill.

The Postmaster General has been indisposed for a day or two, but I understand that he will be in his seat tomorrow. I was speaking to him about these very matters, as the right hon. leader of the Opposition had inquired as to what Bills would be taken up during the bal-lance of the session, and the Postmaster General will probably be able to give his answer to-morrow. I will supply my hon. friend with the required information as soon as the Postmaster General is in his seat.
On motion of Mr. Rogers, House adjourned at 12.30 a.m. Thursday.
